5eb454057e72c34e: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 13 — Malaysia is ready to facilitate any formal request to investigate Speedmatrix Sdn Bhd, said Investment, Trade and Industry Minister Datuk Seri Johari Abdul Ghani.
However, he said, the government is yet to receive any such request.
“If they have a case, they come and check. No problem. We will facilitate,” he told reporters after the launch of MySaham Miti here on Thursday.
Johari said this when asked on whether the government has received a formal request to probe Speedmatrix, a Malaysian unit of Singapore-based cloud computing firm Megaspeed International.
It was reported that Speedmatrix, allegedly linked to the Nvidia chip controversy, might have breached the country’s export restriction.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has admitted to having an affair with a woman linked to Megaspeed International, prompting the US-based chipmaker to announce his immediate resignation as president, CEO and board member pending an independent investigation.

Meanwhile, Johari said he had raised the issue with data centre operators, drawing a distinction between using graphics processing units (GPUs) at a company’s own data centre and re-exporting the chips.

“So far I have already informed all the data centres… Is there anything wrong with Speedmatrix or Megaspeed renting the data centre? If there is nothing wrong and they buy the GPU for their own use in the data centre, then I cannot see what law that we need to use.
“But if there is a restriction in re-exporting that GPU, that is something that we need to look into,” he said. — Bernama

d9bd6f93af7fefb9: NOVEMBER 13 — The world’s health systems are being squeezed from every direction at once. In Davos this year, the WHO’s director-general described an “icy chill” settling over global health: stalled progress, brutal aid cuts, and a long list of threats that no single country can manage alone. In Malaysia, the queues outside public hospitals tell a story familiar to too many nations—a system straining under doctor shortages, uneven distribution, and the quiet erosion of the very workforce that holds everything together .

The question is no longer whether another crisis is coming. It is what shape it will take, and whether we will have the humility to prepare for the threats we can see—and the imagination to prepare for the ones we cannot.

The Lancet Commission’s sweeping new assessment offers a sobering map. It identifies seventeen interlinked catastrophic threats, from antimicrobial resistance and climate change to obesity, poor mental health, and income inequality. Two stand apart for their extinction potential: nuclear conflict and the malicious use of artificial intelligence. The rest are slower, more insidious, and already here. Climate change alone, if warming reaches 4.4°C rather than being limited to 1.8°C, could cost 1.89 billion healthy life years to heat and air pollution. Income inequality, by 2100, could impose a health burden equivalent to twenty-five Covid-19 pandemics .
Various protective face masks are seen in Toulouse, southern France in this file picture taken on May 19, 2020. — AFP pic

Then there is the threat that refuses to stay in the past. Covid-19 has not disappeared. It circulates at low levels globally, its variants still shifting, its surveillance gaps widening as testing and sequencing decline. The WHO assesses the current global risk as moderate, but warns that low vaccine uptake among high-risk groups and insufficient genomic data leave us with “continued uncertainty”. The world cannot afford to treat the next pandemic as a surprise when the warning lights are already blinking.

Meanwhile, the health workforce—the backbone of any response—is being hollowed out. The WHO’s latest safeguards list identifies countries with critical shortages, and recommends against active international recruitment from them. But recommendations are voluntary. Rich nations continue to pull nurses and doctors from poorer ones, draining the very systems that can least afford to lose them. Malaysia’s own experience is instructive: only 6,500 of 12,198 graduate training slots filled as of February, a shortage that forces the ministry to rely on “cluster crisis management” just to keep services running. When the foundation cracks, every other threat becomes harder to meet.
So how should countries respond? Three principles matter.

First, stop treating health as a cost centre and start treating it as infrastructure. The Lancet Commission estimates that action to reduce obesity risk could avert 23.1 billion disability-adjusted life years by 2100. Education improvements could avert 16.1 billion. These are not abstract numbers; they are years of life, years of productivity, years of care that families will not have to give up. Health spending is not charity. It is the precondition for everything else.

Second, rebuild the workforce with intention. Malaysia’s reforms—phasing out the contract system for medical officers, mandating fairer distribution, streamlining training—are a start, but they must be matched by retention strategies that make public service sustainable. Countries cannot simply poach their way out of a shortage. The WHO’s code of practice on health worker recruitment exists for a reason; it needs teeth, and it needs buy-in from the destination countries that benefit most from the current imbalance.

Third, prepare for the unknown while fixing the known. Disease X is not a specific pathogen; it is a placeholder for the certainty that something will emerge. The investments that make sense for pandemic preparedness—surveillance, genomic sequencing, vaccine platforms, community health systems—are the same investments that strengthen routine care. Integration, not duplication, is the only sustainable path.

The SDGs set health as a goal, but health is also the condition for achieving every other goal. A child who is malnourished cannot learn. A mother who dies in childbirth cannot contribute to her community’s economy. A workforce decimated by burnout cannot respond to the next emergency.

The world faces a choice. It can continue to lurch from crisis to crisis, patching systems that were never designed for the pressures they now face. Or it can decide that health is not a line item to be cut when budgets tighten, but the foundation on which everything else is built.

The queues outside Malaysia’s hospitals are a warning. The declining surveillance data on Covid-19 is a warning. The seventeen threats on the Lancet Commission’s list are a warning. The question is whether we will listen before the next crisis forces us to. It would be foolish to ignore such warnings.

e2f6c66aba5aa73b: NOVEMBER 13 — Royal prerogatives are legal powers that are used without requiring parliamentary authority.

Parliament is supreme in the United Kingdom. But historically, there were executive, legislative and judicial powers which would have been exercised by a monarch directly. The majority of the powers have, over time, been abolished, delegated to ministers or replaced by statute.

In so far as it has not been superseded by statute, the royal prerogative, or simply the prerogative, is the power which is utilised by the monarch and its ministers and servants in exercising the functions of government. (See Stair Memorial Encyclopaedia of the Laws of Scotland, Volume 7, The Crown, LexisNexis, 1995)
It is a significant source of constitutional law in the UK, which has no written constitution.
Yet it is a “notoriously difficult concept to define”.
There is no single accepted definition, with various definitions appearing to conflict with each other.

The classic definition is by constitutional theorist A.V. Dicey, who described it as “historically and as a matter of fact nothing else than the residue of discretionary or arbitrary authority which at any given time is legally left in the hands of the crown .... Every act which the executive government can lawfully do without the authority of an Act of Parliament is done in virtue of the prerogative”.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
A screen capture shows the Federal Constitution in both English and Malay displayed on the website of the Attorney General’s Chambers.
The UK Cabinet Manual calls the prerogative the “residual power inherent in the Sovereign, and now exercised mostly on the advice of the Prime Minister and Ministers of the Crown”.
There are four main types of prerogative power (not including two further categories that are statutory but involve the advice of ministers) namely:
Ø Prerogative power exercised by the King alone;
Ø Prerogative power exercised by the King on the advice of ministers;
Ø Prerogative power exercised by ministers;
Ø Prerogative power exercised by the King in Council (the Privy Council);
(See David Torrance, “The royal prerogative and ministerial advice”, House of Commons Library, August 2025))
The prerogative power exercised by the King alone includes the appointment of the prime minister.
The prerogative power exercised by the King on the advice of the minister includes the royal prerogative of mercy (RPM).

The RPM originates in the ancient power vested in the monarch who had the absolute right to exercise mercy on any subject. The original use of the RPM, it is said, arose as a result of the imposition of the death sentence; the RPM then being used to commute such a sentence to a less draconian form of punishment.

Today, the RPM is the power of the monarch to show mercy towards an offender, by mitigating or removing the consequences that follow conviction for an offence. Its use is reflected in the promise to administer justice "in mercy" in the Coronation Oath.
The RPM is also generally restricted to three exceptional situations:

Ø Special remission, a means of reducing the effect of a sentence once it has been imposed, by releasing a prisoner from having to serve some or all of the remainder of his or her sentence in custody. This applies in four circumstances:
– on compassionate grounds;
– provision of information helping to bring others to justice;
– prevention of escape, injury or death; and
– where the prison authorities have miscalculated a release date or released a prisoner early by mistake;
Ø A conditional pardon, which substitutes one type of sentence for another;
Ø A free pardon, which releases a person from the effect of a penalty or a consequence of a sentence it can be used to change any sentence or penalty imposed upon a person.

In Malaysia, 40 years ago, the Supreme Court in the case of Superintendent Of Pudu Prison & Ors v Sim Kie Chon [1986] considered Article 42 of the Federal Constitution as a reiteration of the RPM exercisable on the advice of the appropriate Pardons Board.
The apex court said:

“[T]he power of pardon or otherwise to mete out clemency is an executive power, and in our Constitution the royal prerogative of mercy is expressly preserved by Article 42 of the Constitution and is recognised by its inclusion in Chapter 3 of Part IV thereof as an executive power.”
The apex court went on to approve the statement by Lord President Suffian who delivered the judgment in the case of in Public Prosecutor v Lim Hiang Seoh [1979] as follows:

“It is our considered view that the power of mercy is a high prerogative exercisable by the Yang di-Pertuan Agong or the Ruler of a State or the Yang di-Pertuan Negeri, as the case may be, who acts with the greatest conscience and care and without fear of influence from any quarter.”

Sixteen years later, the apex court in the case of Juraimi Bin Husin v Pardons Board, State Of Pahang & Ors [2002] reiterated that Article 42 is the RPM in Malaysia, rendering it to be “non-justiciable and provided they are validly exercised in accordance with the applicable law, such decisions cannot be brought before the courts for judicial review”.
So, this much is clear: Article 42 of the Federal Constitution preserves the RPM in Malaysia.
Yet the RPM is a prerogative exercised by the King on advice, not by the King alone.

The High Court may well be called to determine whether the RPM is exercised by the King on advice or by the King alone in the Malaysian Bar’s fresh challenge against the Federal Territories Pardons Board’s decision allowing former prime minister Datuk Seri Najib Tun Razak to serve the remainder of his prison sentence in the SRC International Sdn Bhd case under house arrest.

Minister in the Prime Minister’s Department (Law and Institutional Reform) Datuk Seri Azalina Othman Said has rightly said the Bar is entitled to mount such a challenge if it believes it has grounds to question the decision.
Now, what follows immediately after Article 42 is as clear as day as well, and as important.
It is Article 43, which makes provisions on the Cabinet.
Clause (3) of the Article says, in no more than eight words, that the “Cabinet shall be collectively responsible to Parliament”.
As I wrote in “Ministers: Resign or be sacked?" collective responsibility is embedded in the Federal Constitution.
If a member disagrees with the Cabinet’s decision, he or she must still publicly support it. Otherwise, the member must resign.

It is poignant that the RPM and collective responsibility are drafted one after another in the Federal Constitution. These are two British constitutional concepts – one preserved, the other embedded in our supreme law.
If you invoke one, don’t leave out the other.
Articles 42 and 43 are inseparable, like "irama dan lagu, tidak boleh dipisahkan".

5d04d32d1a19679e: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 13 — Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim has been ranked 13th in the 2027 edition of The Muslim 500: The World’s 500 Most Influential Muslims, published by the Jordan-based Royal Islamic Strategic Studies Centre (RISSC).

According to the 18th annual edition accessible at https://themuslim500.com, the publication noted that Anwar assumed office as Malaysia’s 10th Prime Minister in November 2022, leading the Unity Government under the Pakatan Harapan coalition.

The report highlighted that Anwar, who is also Finance Minister, prioritised a robust digital and economic transition strategy for Malaysia under his signature Malaysia Madani framework, placing artificial intelligence, semiconductors, data centres, quantum computing, and the energy transition at the heart of his government’s strategic agenda.

“In June 2026, Anwar highlighted the energy transition as a key pillar of Malaysia’s development agenda, connecting the country’s future energy needs directly to the rapid expansion of its high-tech infrastructure sectors,” it said.

On the regional front, the publication underscored Anwar’s role as a constructive peace broker in South-east Asia, notably his diplomatic initiatives in easing tensions and building trust between Thailand and Cambodia following border clashes in July 2025.

“As Malaysia’s Prime Minister and Asean Chair, he hosted talks between the two countries’ leaders in Putrajaya that helped secure a ceasefire. Anwar helped build trust between Bangkok and Phnom Penh, reinforcing Malaysia’s image as a constructive peace broker in South-east Asia,” the report said.

In addition, The Muslim 500 recognised Anwar as one of the world’s most outspoken heads of state regarding the Palestinian cause, maintaining unyielding state support for civilian protection and humanitarian access in Gaza.

“Taking an aggressive international stance, Anwar announced to the Malaysian Parliament that the country is spearheading a core international coalition drafting a formal resolution to expel Israel from the United Nations. Anwar reiterated that Malaysia’s absolute non-recognition of Israel is permanent,” it said.

According to the publication, Anwar’s meetings with Hamas officials, including its late leader Ismail Haniyeh, drew public pushback from Western countries. However, Anwar dismissed the criticism, asserting Malaysia’s sovereign right to determine its own foreign policy.

Beyond his political leadership, the citation traced Anwar’s early activism as founder and president of the Malaysian Islamic Youth Movement (ABIM) in 1971, as well as his career in major Cabinet portfolios, including Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister, during the 1990s.
It also highlighted his contributions to academia, noting that he had held visiting academic positions at St Antony’s College, Oxford, Johns Hopkins University and Georgetown University.

“He is a co-founder of the International Institute of Islamic Thought (IIIT) established in the United States in 1981. Furthermore, he served as the Chancellor of the International Islamic University Malaysia (IIUM) from 1983 to 1988, and has received numerous international honorary degrees,” it said.

In the 2027 edition, the top spot is jointly held by Saudi Arabia’s King Salman bin Abdul-Aziz Al-Saud and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Pakistan’s Prime Minister Mian Muhammad Shehbaz Sharif and Chief of Army Staff General Syed Asim Munir, alongside Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.

Other prominent South-east Asian leaders listed in the Top 50 include Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto at 16th place, Nahdlatul Ulama chairman Yahya Cholil Staquf (21st) and Indonesian scholar Habib Luthfi bin Yahya (31st).

Meanwhile, Palestinian paediatrician and Kamal Adwan Hospital director Dr Hussam Abu Safiya, who had been held in Israeli detention without charge since December 2024, was named The Muslim 500’s Man of the Year for 2027 and ranked 50th on the list. — Bernama

9740b7bb9dd8debf: MILAN, Nov 13 — Zinedine Zidane was unimpressed with his side’s defensive display after suffering his first defeat as France head coach against Italy yesterday, but described the setback as “part of the process”.

Les Bleus took an early lead at San Siro through Michael Olise to put one foot in the UEFA Nations League quarter-finals, but were pegged back by a Francesco Pio Esposito double and Davide Frattesi strike.
Italy seized control of the game in the second half after the two sides went in level at the break following an opening period dominated by Zidane’s side.

Frattesi’s goal arrived three minutes after Sebastiano Esposito had missed a penalty, and France conceded a second spot kick, converted by the younger Esposito brother, to take the game beyond the visitors.
“We started well and we were good in possession, but in the second half we ran into difficulties, especially defensively,” Zidane told a press conference.

Asked if the team lacked courage, he replied: “No, quite the opposite. We stayed in the game, we did well in possession, especially in the first half, but in the second half we caved in a bit, especially after 2-1. It’s part of the process.”
France were twice denied by the woodwork and had 60 per cent possession and 18 attempts during an entertaining game as they slipped behind Italy into second place on head-to-head record in Group A1.
Zidane’s side host Turkey, who have failed to pick up a single point thus far, in their final game on Sunday, while Italy travel to Belgium, who are one point behind in third.
“The most important thing is creating chances,” Zidane added.
“Hitting the post had an impact, but I’m not disappointed. I would have been if we hadn’t created good possession. What we need to analyse is why we weren’t at the right level off the ball.”
Mancini tips Esposito for record

France were without star attackers Kylian Mbappe and Ousmane Dembele for the trip to Milan, but Zidane denied that their absence impacted the performance and revealed that Real Madrid striker Mbappe could return against Turkey.
“I think all the players were focused. As I said, we were a little less focused and less effective in the second half,” Zidane said.
“I hope (Mbappe) can play against Turkey. That is the plan, we decided not to risk him tonight because he had a little problem.”
Italy coach Roberto Mancini’s impressive start to his second spell continued as his side moved top and stretched their unbeaten run to four games.

Esposito’s double caught the attention as the Inter Milan striker took his international tally to nine goals in 14 games, and Mancini believes he could even eye the long-standing national record held by 1968 European champion Gigi Riva.
“Let’s hope he scores a lot more goals,” Mancini said.
“Gigi Riva has been up there on 35 for a lifetime. Let’s hope someone surpasses him. We need goals from Pio and the others too, but he can score a lot.”
Esposito could have had a hat-trick had his older brother not taken - and missed - Italy’s first penalty of the match during the second half, a moment Mancini revealed was not part of the plan.
“Pio is first choice and then Sebastiano. It was a family thing,” Mancini laughed. — AFP

24eca933b484a823: JAKARTA, Nov 13 — Wildfires that consumed vast swathes of Indonesia this year were driven largely by a strong El Nino, fuelled by climate change and decades of natural landscape destruction, researchers said today.

El Nino was largely to blame for an extreme lack of rainfall in the Southeast Asian archipelago from July to October, reducing seasonal rainfall by about half, according to a report by scientists from the World Weather Attribution (WWA) group.
Climate change contributed by driving up temperatures.
“Seasonal temperatures from August to October were dominated by climate change — primarily from the burning of fossil fuels — which made the seasonal heat about 1.6°C hotter,” said the report.
“Human-induced warming made these (fire-prone) atmospheric conditions about three times more likely as well as more intense.”
The researchers also pointed to deforestation and peatland drainage for agriculture, mining and logging as major contributors to the fire disaster.
Smoke from the wildfires made hundreds of thousands ill in Indonesia from breathing in toxic haze and exposed many more in neighbouring countries to dangerously high air pollution levels.

“Indonesia’s landscapes have changed dramatically over the last 30 years, with extensive peatland drainage and deforestation creating landscapes that can be extremely vulnerable to ignition,” said meteorologist Pramudhian Firdaus of the FLARE Wildfire Research group.
“These findings show how both emissions reductions and sustained forest and peatland protection are important in reducing future risk.”
Wildfires have burned through 2.88 million hectares (7.1 million acres) so far in 2026, according to the Nusantara Atlas deforestation monitor.
The burned area figure — 18 times the size of London — increased nearly a million hectares in a month.
The Indonesian government has not confirmed or rejected the figure nor released its own estimate of area burnt since July.
Indonesia experiences fires every dry season, but this year’s blazes have been particularly severe. — AFP

1aeb3c194ffe1012: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 13 — Malaysian director Edmund Yeo brings a beautiful pathos to his adaptation of Li Zi Shu's acclaimed The Age of Goodbyes.

Li herself was unsure about her book's adaptability as it spins from one era to the next, back and forth, while somehow also weaving in two sets of twins, born in different eras with almost matching fates.
But it is not the twins that form the centrepiece here; instead it is Taiwanese actress Vivian Sung who carries the weight of the film on her very elegant shoulders.
Sung spent time in Malaysia so she could master a passable local accent in the various Chinese languages she had to speak in the film.
The actress switched between Mandarin, Cantonese and even Hokkien with a convincing fluidity.
She is immensely watchable as Du Li An, a small town girl who ends up marrying the local taikor.
Du's heart, however, belongs to Yip Lin Sang (Stanley Yau Sze Chun), a man on a mission to break a family curse but Yip leaves town one day without even saying goodbye.
What happens when a man with the same surname, but calls himself Yip Mong Sang comes to Ipoh, bearing exactly the same face as Du's former paramour?
Are there really two Yip men? Why does Du speak Mandarin with one man and Cantonese with the other? Why are all her qi pao amazing?
If the film gets confusing at times, it's enough to just keep your eye on Sung because without the strength she brings to her portrayal, the film would be far less interesting.
Not that the other actors don't pull their weight — Yau is remarkably convincing in his portrayal of two different characters with great supporting performances from Li Xuan Siow and Liu Tzu-chuan.
Li and Liu play youngsters whose lives are forever marked by the decisions of their caregivers and they bring both a charming innocence and convincing grief to their roles.
Also adding necessary local flavour is Malaysian actor Steve Yap, a veteran of the local scene.
Like the book, the film makes references to the May 13, 1969 riots in Malaysia but also swings back to various parts of Malaysian Chinese history.

That includes the local Communist party, Chinese immigrant workers, past transgressions of British colonisers (one character speaks of his father being killed by British enforcers) but Yeo is not here to preach or overdramatise.

Brief vignettes of history take their place in the woven narrative as the film often see-saws between the past and present and while the threads can be a lot to take in, by the end of it, the film does reward you for paying attention.

I am not going to spoil the last 10 minutes of the film but I will say that it is very Malaysian in its references that will go right over the heads of non-Malaysian audiences while not detracting from the narrative.
It is important that films like The Age of Goodbyes exist; that they tell stories to mark, for future generations, the histories, hardships and the simple humanity of their forebears.
Yet another good reason to watch the film is if you are Ipoh-born because of the film's loving portrayal of Ipoh, painting its limestone caves, hills and fields in a near-incandescent glow.
On a side note, I did ask Yeo where Sung's qi pao were from and he said the Malaysian/Taiwanese team commissioned them from a Taiwanese artisan.

The film however falls under the 18 classification so best avoid taking your under-18 cousins to this film. You can probably bring your slightly prudish aunt along as the reason for that rating is... mildy steamy kissing scenes.
No nudity, no gore, no acts of violence that could be triggering but most importantly, no cuts so you can enjoy the film without feeling like you blinked and someone fast-forwarded.

The Age of Goodbyes is Edmund Yeo's most accessible film yet and one that will have a deeper resonance with Malaysians in its treatment of history, and how some decisions will have consequences that reverberate even now.
If you're keen on some old Ipoh nostalgia, head over to your nearest cinema as the film has only just opened on November 12.
b322c325ba253ec3: WASHINGTON, Nov 13 — US President Donald Trump said yesterday that former Apple CEO Tim Cook should replace Jensen Huang at Nvidia, after Huang quit over revelations of two affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.
“Now that Nvidia CEO JENSEN HUANG, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place — TIM COOK of Apple,” Trump said on his Truth Social network.
Trump has no formal say in who should run chip giant Nvidia, which is at the centre of the AI revolution, but his extraordinary intervention underscores his close ties to both Huang and Cook.
During his second presidency, Trump has treated Nvidia co-founder Huang as a close adviser, even bringing him on board Air Force One for a state visit to China in May.
After allegations emerged about Huang’s ties to Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, Trump this week defended the Nvidia boss and said he had no idea Alice Huang was allegedly spying for Beijing.
Trump added that Jensen Huang, who is not related to Alice Huang, was “suffering greatly” and described the Taiwanese-born tech boss as “an amazing guy.”
But Trump still faces questions over what he knew about the allegations — and when he knew.

The New York Times reported earlier this week that Trump was informed about the allegations by Secretary of State Marco Rubio aboard Air Force One in May — shortly before picking up Huang in Alaska for the flight to Beijing.
Cook — who stood down as Apple CEO in September but remains executive chair of its board of directors — is another of the tech titans who have swarmed around the White House since Trump’s return.

In August 2025, Cook appeared in the Oval Office with Trump to announce that Apple would increase its investments in the US to US$600 billion, as Trump threatened huge tariffs on tech products made abroad.
He also brought one of the flashy presents that Trump loves — a custom-engraved glass piece made by iPhone glassmaker Corning, set in a 24-karat gold base.
The gift helped smooth relations between Cook and Trump, who had repeatedly criticised Apple in the past for not manufacturing its iPhones in the US.
Cook also accompanied Trump to China in May, and both he and Huang attended the lavish state banquet that the US president held at the White House for Xi in September. — AFP

38f938114eae97f2: KOTA KINABALU, Nov 13 — The Sabah government is open to credible investments in the technology sector, including the development of artificial intelligence (AI) data centres, but every investment proposal must undergo rigorous evaluation to ensure that the interests of the people and the state’s basic infrastructure requirements are not compromised.

Sabah Chief Minister Datuk Seri Hajiji Noor said the state government’s openness to investments and strategic partnerships must be accompanied by due diligence and responsible decision-making, particularly for large-scale projects requiring substantial energy and water resources.

“However, this openness must always be accompanied by due diligence and responsible decision-making processes,” he said in a statement issued by the Chief Minister’s Department Media and Communications Office today.

The statement was issued in conjunction with the signing ceremony of a memorandum of understanding (MoU) for the proposed establishment of Sabah’s first Artificial Intelligence Data Centre (AIDC) here yesterday, with Hajiji’s speech delivered by Deputy Chief Minister II and Sabah Finance Minister Datuk Seri Masidi Manjun.

Hajiji said the signing of the MoU between North AIDC Sdn Bhd and several global partners was an encouraging initial step, but the project’s actual success would depend on careful planning, comprehensive evaluation and the benefits it could bring to Sabah.
“However, the true measure of progress is what happens after this signing, namely careful planning, proper evaluation and meaningful outcomes for Sabah,” he said.

Hajiji stressed that the signing of an MoU did not mean that a project had obtained state government approval, adding that every proposal must still fulfil all conditions and requirements stipulated by the relevant agencies.

He said the evaluation of proposed data centre developments must take into account technical and financial viability, electricity and water supply requirements, cooling technology, environmental protection, land use and connectivity.

He said developers must also work closely with authorities and utility providers to ensure that the development of such facilities did not undermine the reliability of essential services required by the people.
“Modern digital economies should strengthen Sabah’s infrastructure, rather than place unnecessary additional pressure on it,” he said.

Meanwhile, Hajiji said data centre development could create opportunities for local companies in engineering, construction, telecommunications, logistics and support services, particularly during the construction phase.

In this regard, he encouraged project developers to provide opportunities for local contractors, collaborate with universities and technical institutions, and introduce apprenticeship programmes to enable Sabah’s youth to acquire skills in the digital technology sector.

Hajiji said developments in AI and cloud computing offered Sabah opportunities to strengthen its participation in the digital economy, but these efforts must go hand in hand with addressing basic infrastructure problems still faced by some residents of the state.

He added that the experience of other states, including Johor in data centre development, could serve as a guide, particularly in utility management, environmental protection and the interests of local communities. — Bernama
c318e4b2c7068709: LONDON, Nov 13 — US head coach Mauricio Pochettino is set to be appointed as the new manager of Manchester United after the struggling English giants sacked Michael Carrick yesterday.

Pochettino is expected to leave his role with the USA following their two-legged CONCACAF Nations League quarter-final on tomorrow and Tuesday in a move that will see United trigger a release clause worth some US$10 million to secure the Argentine’s services.
Pochettino, who signed a contract extension to remain with the US through to the 2030 World Cup just three months ago, is due to hold a pre-match press conference on today.

Former United captain Carrick led the team to an impressive third-place finish in the Premier League last season, but they have taken just eight points from 10 games in the current campaign and are in the relegation zone.
The club confirmed in a statement yesterday that it had parted ways with the 45-year-old, following mounting speculation he would be axed during the international break.
“After a disappointing start to the season, the club has come to the extremely difficult conclusion that a change is necessary in order to achieve our ambitions,” United said.

“Michael is, and always will be, a Manchester United legend. Just as he did as a player, he has conducted himself with the highest standards of dedication and professionalism throughout his time back with the club.”
Carrick impressed after taking over as interim boss following Ruben Amorim’s acrimonious exit in January, leading United to Champions League qualification.
He was rewarded with a two-year permanent deal but, hampered by the club’s underwhelming recruitment in the summer transfer window, his side have endured a steep decline this season.
Carrick has struggled to maintain discipline, dropping captain Bruno Fernandes after he criticised his manager’s tactics following a 4-1 thrashing at Champions League debutants Como.
And defender Lisandro Martinez spoke out against the club’s hierarchy over their lack of top-quality signings.

Carrick’s final game in charge was a chaotic 4-4 draw against Aston Villa on Sunday, after which he stressed he would not walk away despite a paltry record of three wins from 15 games in all competitions this season.
It is believed Carrick’s future was decided on Wednesday during a meeting in Monaco involving co-owner Jim Ratcliffe, chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox.
‘Disgusting’
Pochettino has extensive experience of the Premier League following spells in charge of Southampton, Tottenham and Chelsea, and he also coached Paris Saint-Germain.
Carrick, who won multiple trophies as a midfielder in the club’s golden era under Alex Ferguson, is the seventh permanent manager to be dismissed by the club since the Scot retired in 2013.
Former United captain Gary Neville, who played alongside Carrick, said his old team-mate had been treated appallingly.

“It’s just quite simply disgusting,” Neville told Sky Sports. “That falls well below the standard of what you would expect in any other business. In any other industry it would be constructive dismissal and you’d be getting sued.”

The Manchester United Supporters’ Trust said Carrick’s departure marked “another depressing moment”, pinning the blame on majority owners the Glazer family and minority shareholder Ratcliffe, with the club yet to win a Premier League title since the end of the Ferguson era.

“The Glazers’ debt-funded takeover continues to burden the club,” MUST said in a statement. “When (Ratcliffe’s) INEOS came in they promised sporting excellence, but yet with repeated changes in football leadership we have seen anything but.”
United’s next game is against fierce rivals Liverpool at Anfield on November 22. — AFP
940d3e88a37de283: SHAH ALAM, Nov 13 — Weekends are the perfect time to explore far-flung places like Kota Kemuning for a bowl of handmade Cendol (RM6.90) at this unlikely snack shop peddling old school biscuits like pastel Gem biscuits side-by-side with East Coast fish crackers.

At this shop with the unforgettable name of Tang Tang Tang Tang Enterprise, the bowl of finely shaved ice drizzled with sweet-smelling, creamy santan (most probably from the first squeeze of top grade grated coconut) and just a touch of gula Melaka syrup from a squeeze bottle, is covered with light green plump cendol jelly.

The top grade cendol jelly, completely different from the skinny factory made ones, is made from a thick paste of mung beans and rice flour mixed with pandan juice which is then grated over a bowl of ice water to form soft, stubby green jelly that has a mild pandan aroma.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
‘Cendol’ jelly can be paired with soft cooked kidney beans (left). Drizzle how much ‘gula Melaka’ syrup (right) you like over your bowl of ‘cendol’. — Picture by Lee Khang Yi
Soft, cooked, elongated kidney beans also share the bowl with the cendol jelly.
Haters will say the kidney beans aren't needed, as the cendol jelly is good enough but fans will protest and demand their soft presence.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Mee Hoon Kuih is a must in this area where dough pieces are paired with a wholesome ‘ikan bilis’ broth dotted with fried shallots and fried ‘ikan bilis’. — Picture by Lee Khang Yi
From the shopfront, it's hard to see inside because bamboo chicks shield the place from the glaring sunlight.
Once inside, I found about 30 people sitting at small tables; most of them were acquainted with each other as neighbours or even church members since it was Sunday.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Long, wide strands of the dough from Mee Hoon Kuih taste silky soft on the tongues. — Picture by Lee Khang Yi
Two ladies from Melaka are at the helm; the elder one with grey hair keeps an eagle eye on the tables, ensuring they turn around quickly while another rushes orders out from the small kitchen.
The menu is ordinary but features guaranteed favourites cooked from the heart, like mee hoon kuih, nasi lemak, bubur cha cha, red bean with pulut hitam and their best-selling cendol.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Nasi Lemak with Turmeric Chicken travelled home with the writer, and it’s a great version with ‘santan’-rich fluffy rice served with turmeric boneless chicken, spicy ‘sambal’, fried egg and ‘ikan bilis’. — Picture by Lee Khang Yi

A smart partnership with Goh Abdullah, a Chinese Muslim whom many in Kota Kemuning know for his Penang favourites like white curry mee, pasembur and cucur udang, extends the choices because Tang Tang Tang Tang Enterprise's small kitchen is unable to handle them.
You need to walk down the corridor to find their place tucked in a corner to place your order and pay. Helpful staff will send your food straight to your table.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Behold the magnificent bowl of Assam Laksa from Goh Abdullah, thick with pounded fish with tangy, spicy notes and freshened up with pineapple, raw onions, cucumber and red chillies. — Picture by Lee Khang Yi
Mee Hoon Kuih (RM9.90) typically uses hand-torn dough pieces, but this place takes a shortcut with long strips of dough, likely pressed flat by a machine.
This version is exceptional — the long pieces have a silky soft texture that pairs well with the light, ikan bilis-based broth, which can be accompanied by fried ikan bilis and fried shallots.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
The space inside Tang Tang Tang Tang Enterprise (left) is small and intimate. Shop for snacks like fish crackers and biscuits from your long forgotten childhood (right). — Picture by Lee Khang Yi
I was curious about the Nasi Lemak with Turmeric Chicken (RM9.90) since everyone was happily tucking into it so I packed a portion to take home.

It turned out to be a good move to be greedy, as the rice is fluffy and full of santan, hitting your nose with its sweet notes, which paired well with the turmeric boneless chicken, spicy sambal, fried ikan bilis and a well fried egg.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Tucked in a corner of Jalan Suasana 1, you will find Goh Abdullah, a veteran of the Kota Kemuning food scene (left). You can’t miss the bright red signage to this tiny snack shop converted into an eatery (right). — Picture by Lee Khang Yi

Penang Asam Laksa (RM8.50) from Goh Abdullah was wonderfully thick with pounded fish, featuring the magical alchemy of sourness from tamarind and freshness from pineapple, cucumber, lettuce, sliced raw onions and red chilies.
This dish demanded that every bit, including the soft rice noodles, be scraped clean from the bowl.
As the spiciness lingers on the tongue after the bowl is emptied, have another bowl of cendol or their refreshing Passion Fruit Soda (RM5.80), made with fresh fruit pulp combined with soda water.
Tang Tang Tang Tang Enterprise
Jalan Suasana 1,
Kota Kemuning, Shah Alam.
Open: 11am to 5pm.
Closed on the third Tuesday and Wednesday of every month. For November, they will be closed on November 17 and 18.

Jalan Suasana 1,
Kota Kemuning, Shah Alam.

ca9e741d9f2eecdf: PARIS, Nov 13 — England secured their place in the Nations League quarter-finals with a 2-1 victory over Croatia yesterday, while Zinedine Zidane suffered his first defeat as France coach as his side lost away to Italy.
Harry Kane marked his record-breaking 126th appearance for England by scoring the winning goal from the penalty spot at Wembley, taking his international tally to 92 goals.
Morgan Rogers put England ahead in the first half before a mistake by Jarell Quansah allowed Petar Sucic to equalise for Croatia on the hour mark.
England regained the lead when Ivan Smolcic wrestled Quansah to the ground at a corner, with Kane converting the resulting penalty after a VAR review.
Thomas Tuchel’s side moved to 12 points from five matches in Group A3, ensuring they will go through to the quarter-finals next March.
“Good win. We wanted this win desperately and I think we deserved it,” Tuchel told ITV.
“We got the job done and it was important because it was a special occasion for Harry and he scored the winner, so perfect evening.”
Spain top the section on 15 points after a 2-0 win over the Czech Republic in Prague, their fifth straight victory in the competition.

Alex Baena’s penalty and a late goal from Marc Pubill extended Spain’s unbeaten run in competitive matches to 44 and set up a showdown with England in Madrid on Sunday, which will decide the group winners.
The Czechs remain without a point and finished with 10 men after captain Ladislav Krejci was sent off.
Italy turn tables on France
Italy came from behind to beat France 3-1 in Milan and hand Zidane his first defeat since taking charge of Les Bleus.
France were without Kylian Mbappe and Ousmane Dembele due to injury but Michael Olise pounced on a loose pass from Gianluigi Donnarumma to fire them ahead on 10 minutes.
Francesco Pio Esposito steered in Nicolo Cambiaghi’s pass to bring Italy level before France twice hit the post through Bradley Barcola and Rayan Cherki.
Sebastiano Esposito blazed a second-half penalty wide for Italy, but Roberto Mancini’s side did not rue that miss as Davide Frattesi powered home Federico Dimarco’s cut-back.
Francesco Pio Esposito then doubled his tally for the night, succeeding where his older brother had failed by converting a penalty after Dayot Upamecano fouled substitute Antonio Vergara.
Zidane put the loss down to “part of the learning process”.
“You mustn’t change anything just because of a defeat,” he said.
Italy climbed above France at the top of Group A1 on head-to-head record. Both teams have 10 points going into the final round of games, with Belgium just one point adrift.
Belgium host Italy on Sunday and France are at home to Turkey.
Zidane said Mbappe could return for the game in Bordeaux.
“I hope he’ll be available on Sunday. That was the plan, that’s what we want,” he said.
Turkey slid to a fifth straight loss as they went down 2-1 to Belgium in Izmir.

Arda Guler’s magnificent free-kick put Turkey ahead under new coach and former midfielder Sergen Yalcin, but Belgium struck twice in quick succession with goals from Kevin De Bruyne and Charles De Ketelaere to come away with victory. — AFP

743781c83a2ca3d1: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 13 — The government is expected to launch the second phase of the Refugee Registration Document (DPP) programme soon, targeting United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) cardholders not held at Immigration Detention Depots (DTIs).

Deputy Prime Minister Datuk Seri Dr Ahmad Zahid Hamidi said the programme to register Myanmar refugee communities nationwide remained in its first phase, targeting individuals at Immigration Detention Depots (DTIs).

“The government is also studying whether movement controls should be imposed on these groups, while considering national security and sovereignty interests as well as human rights,” he said in a written reply posted on the Parliament website.

He was responding to a question from Aminolhuda Hassan (PH-Sri Gading) on the status of preparing and presenting a comprehensive refugee management plan to the Cabinet, as well as a proposal to table the policy framework in the Dewan Rakyat.

Ahmad Zahid said the National Security Council (MKN), Prime Minister’s Department, was working closely with relevant ministries and agencies to hold engagement sessions to obtain feedback and formulate appropriate measures to address issues concerning refugees in Malaysia.

Meanwhile, in response to a question from Datuk Seri Dr Shahidan Kassim (PN-Arau), Ahmad Zahid said refugees had entered Malaysia through syndicates at land and sea borders rather than through authorised or gazetted International Entry Points.

He said the government was also stepping up efforts to strengthen MKN Directive No. 23 on the Policy and Mechanism for the Management of Refugees and Asylum Seekers (2023 Revision), which the Prime Minister signed on June 14, 2023.

He said coordinated operations involving security agencies, enforcement bodies and local authorities were also being conducted to tackle violations by foreign migrants, including gang-related activities.

“The implementation of the DPP for registration purposes, together with integrated operations by security and enforcement agencies, is expected to help curb negative influences aimed at manipulating existing communities,” he said.

The Deputy Prime Minister was replying to Shahidan’s question on action taken by the government to tackle the entry of Myanmar refugees allegedly involved in gang-related activities, especially at Selayang Market, and measures to prevent the exploitation of the community. — Bernama
785b4c4b6a2e4b63: SAN FRANCISCO (US), Nov 12 — Jensen Huang, the leather-jacketed architect of the artificial intelligence boom, resigned as chief executive of Nvidia yesterday after revelations of two extramarital affairs, including one with a woman accused of spying for China.

Chief financial officer Colette Kress, who joined Nvidia in 2013 after nearly 25 years at companies including Cisco and Microsoft, will serve as interim CEO while the board searches for a successor, ending Huang’s 33 years at the helm of the company he co-founded.
Huang, 63, also gave up his board seat. Nvidia did not give a reason for his departure.

Huang was a central figure in the boom set off by the launch of OpenAI’s ChatGPT in 2022, with Nvidia’s processors, once designed for video game graphics, becoming the crucial ingredient for building AI models.
He was also a close informal adviser to President Donald Trump on AI.
Nvidia shares fell as much as 13 per cent following the announcement before paring losses to about four per cent, wiping roughly US$450 billion off the company’s value since the weekend.

Dan Ives of investment bank Yorkville Ives called it “a dark day for Nvidia and the US tech industry,” but said the board had done what it needed to: “rip off the band-aid and take Nvidia into its next chapter without him.”

The board named Harvey Jones, a former chief executive of chip design software firm Synopsys, as chair, and said it expected the company’s operations and product roadmap “to continue without interruption.”
Trump, who had stood by Huang throughout the scandal, said former Apple boss Tim Cook should take over.
“A Legend replaces a Legend!” Trump said on his Truth Social network.
Huang remains Nvidia’s largest individual shareholder, with a stake of about 3.6 per cent, according to the company’s most recent filing.
For many in Silicon Valley, the departure recalls that of Steve Jobs, who was pushed out of Apple by its board in 1985 and returned 12 years later to take the company to new heights.
Two alleged affairs

Huang, who has been married to his wife Lori for more than 40 years, admitted on Sunday to an affair, reportedly with Alice Huang, a former senior executive at Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed. The two are not related.
US intelligence reportedly circulated a memo this spring alleging she was an asset of China’s Ministry of State Security. Beijing has rejected the allegations.

Singapore said yesterday it had barred Alice Huang, a Chinese national, from re-entering the country in February for giving investigators inaccurate information about her role at Megaspeed, though she was not investigated for espionage.
Nvidia’s board opened a probe on Sunday into reporting that Huang had been the target of a “foreign intelligence effort,” while saying it retained confidence in him.
But on Wednesday, The New York Times reported a second affair, citing video of Huang being affectionate with Nvidia’s vice president of health care, Kimberly Powell.
US-China tech race
At the heart of the spy allegations is the race between the US and China for supremacy in an industry widely seen as the next industrial revolution.

Key US lawmakers, including Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer, called yesterday for answers on what the Trump administration knew about Huang’s ties to a suspected Chinese intelligence asset, days before Trump travels to China for a summit.
Reports allege the Commerce Department under Secretary Howard Lutnick may have failed to act on suspicions that Megaspeed was helping reroute restricted Nvidia technology to China.

Singapore’s home ministry said it had repeatedly sought information from the US Justice Department and FBI on a US server supplier during its Megaspeed probe, but “received limited information or assistance.” — AFP
d464d85e89c05cf5: LIMA: Pope Leo XIV met six victims of clerical abuse in Peru Thursday, including some linked to the once-powerful and now-disbanded Catholic society, Sodalitium Christianae Vitae.
The US-born pope is on a nostalgic return to the nation he calls his "homeland" and knows the abuse scandal well from the nearly two decades he worked in Peru as a missionary and bishop.

Leo spent over an hour with the victims, meeting "each person individually, listening to their stories of suffering and their pain", and "thanked them for their invaluable testimony", the Vatican said.

Together, "they reflected on how to foster a shift in mindset – by listening to victims, seeking the truth, pursuing paths toward healing, and committing to the creation of safe environments," it said.

Sodalitium Christianae Vitae (SCV), a lay society founded in the 1970s that was widespread in Latin America, was shut down in 2025 by Leo's predecessor Francis after years of allegations of sexual, physical and psychological abuse, as well as corruption.
Before he was elected Pope Leo XIV, Robert Francis Prevost was the bishop designated to hear from SCV victims, who said he was supportive of their claims.
'Pain'

In an address to bishops earlier Thursday, Leo described the "pain" caused by Catholic clerical abuse and said the Church must make "amends" to victims and foster "a culture of prevention and protection."
Clerical abuse, a global scourge, was "a reality that has caused us so much pain", the 71-year-old said.
In April 2026, the Vatican announced plans to set up a "listening channel" in Lima for victims and use assets seized from the lay movement to compensate them.
Renzo Orbegozo, a 50-year-old victim, told AFP they were seeking "comprehensive reparation".
"Many require psychological and medical support, as well as social reintegration - all of which, ultimately, translates into financial assistance," he said.

On the eve of the pope's South America tour, the US-based nonprofit Bishop Accountability presented a list in Lima of 77 members of the Peruvian clergy it said had been publicly accused of abusing minors.
Anne Barrett Doyle, co-director of the group, called on Leo to implement "zero tolerance" of abusers.
'Knows Peruvians' needs'
The head of the 1.4 billion Catholics has not shied away from tackling sensitive political and social topics during his three-nation Latin American tour.
Pilgrim Pedro Campos said Leo was "a member of our country who... knows the needs of all Peruvians."
At a speech later to some 40,000 people on the challenges facing Peruvians, the pontiff slammed "machismo" attitudes and said violence against women was "a reality that wounds all of humanity."
There was no excuse for "an unequal sharing of domestic responsibilities or the subordination of one spouse to the other," he said.
Chicago-born Leo was given a raucous reception by crowds lining the streets, chanting his name.
Thousands of people – including children dressed as the pope or as bishops – lined up for a glimpse of the pope as he drove by in the popemobile.
'Steep ascents'
The intense trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru comes just weeks after the pope had surgery for lung cancer, but he shows no sign of flagging.

In his speech, Leo made fond references to Peru's landscape and culture, telling the Catholic clergy to think of their mission as a difficult but rewarding walk, like the path that leads to Machu Picchu.
He compared the Catholic mission to the "steep ascents" of the Inca Trail in Peru.
The trail, an ancient network of routes that traverses much of the Andes, "is not to be walked alone," he cautioned.
During his tenure in Peru, Prevost worked in poor and remote northern areas, and remained close to local communities during periods of hardship, visiting them sometimes on horseback.
"Walking together fosters communion," he said.
Six days in Peru will see Leo travel from the deep Amazon to the high Andes. He will visit Cuzco, at more than 3,400 metres (11,000 feet) elevation, which will test his recovery from lung surgery.
He will also make an emotional return to Chiclayo, the northern city where he was bishop for a decade.
baa33061ab33e157: PETALING JAYA: Former prime minister Najib Razak’s house arrest may benefit Umno at tomorrow’s Melaka state election, but it may not translate into broader electoral support for the party in other states.

Najib, 73, arrived at his home in Taman Duta, Kuala Lumpur, on Tuesday night to serve the remainder of his six-year prison sentence in the SRC International case, having previously been in Kajang prison since Aug 23, 2022.
On Wednesday, PAS deputy president Tuan Ibrahim Tuan Man said the issue had given Umno momentum ahead of the Melaka polls and could sustain the party through to the 16th general election (GE16).
Analysts say the development is more likely to galvanise existing supporters to vote for Barisan Nasional (BN) than attract new voters ahead of the 16th general election (GE16).
Tawfik Yaakub said Najib was still an influential figure in Melaka, and he agreed with Tuan Ibrahim that the former Umno president’s house arrest could give Umno a boost at tomorrow’s election.
However, the Universiti Malaya academic said the momentum might not carry through to GE16 due to differences in demographics and political culture across states.

He said the issue might be viewed differently in Selangor and Penang, potentially undermining Umno’s efforts to win over voters and rebuild support in the two states, where the party has suffered significant losses since 2008.
“Umno has a strong grassroots presence in Melaka and the advantage of leading the state government,” he told FMT.
“But in Selangor and Penang, particularly in urban areas, voters tend to focus more on issues of integrity, reforms and the economy.
“What works in Melaka may not necessarily work in other states because voters do not share the same sentiments towards Najib.”
Political optimism, not reality
Ahmad Zaharuddin Sani Ahmad Sabri of Global Asia Consulting described Tuan Ibrahim’s remarks as reflecting political optimism rather than the reality of voter behaviour.
He said the house arrest issue might revive enthusiasm among Umno’s grassroots, particularly those who remained loyal to Najib, but was unlikely to attract new voters.
“Will people struggling with the cost of living change their political preferences because a former prime minister has been moved to a different place to serve his sentence?”
Risk for Umno
Meanwhile, Tawfik cautioned that Najib’s house arrest could be a double-edged sword for Umno if the party became too reliant on sentiments surrounding its former president.
“Heading into GE16, Umno needs to prove that it has a reform agenda, new leadership and solutions to the problems facing the people,” he said.
Zaharuddin warned that relying on the issue of Najib’s house arrest could undermine Umno’s efforts to restore the public’s confidence in the party, particularly among younger voters seeking change.
“Umno must not end up succeeding in bringing Najib home but failing to bring voters back to Umno.”

In January 2024, the then Yang di-Pertuan Agong, Al-Sultan Abdullah Sultan Ahmad Shah, halved Najib’s 12-year prison sentence in the SRC International case and reduced his RM210 million fine to RM50 million under a royal pardon.
In September, the current Yang di-Pertuan Agong, Sultan Ibrahim, granted Najib a conditional pardon, allowing him to serve the remainder of his sentence under house arrest until Aug 23, 2028.
The release was subject to Najib’s payment of the RM50 million fine, which Umno settled with funds raised through a donation drive.
593fbf29f321f100: SINGAPORE: Wildfires that hit large parts of Indonesia from August to October and plunged much of Southeast Asia into hazardous smoke were made much worse by "record-breaking" heat caused by human-induced climate change, scientists said on Friday.

While a very strong El Niño was the dominant factor in determining the extremely low levels of rainfall across Indonesia from July, human-induced climate change contributed around 1.6 degrees Celsius of additional heat during the fire season, said a report by climate research group World Weather Attribution.

"The conditions that we saw this year would simply just not have happened in a world without the human contribution to climate change, even with the very strong El Niño that we're seeing," said Theodore Keeping, a researcher into wildfires and extreme weather at Imperial College London who contributed to the report.

"You have multiple different drivers changing in different ways, but what we can say with very high confidence is that the driving weather conditions of these fires are getting more severe," he told a briefing.
Pramudhian Firdaus, a wildfire researcher at Melbourne University, said September 2026 was Indonesia's fifth-driest September since 1991, with rainfall below normal levels across 84% of the country.
Decades of land-use change, involving extensive deforestation and the draining of flammable peatland to make way for industry and agriculture, also compounded this year's fire outbreaks.

"Indonesian landscapes have changed dramatically over the last 30 years, with extensive peatland drainage and deforestation creating a landscape that is extremely vulnerable to ignition," Firdaus said.

According to data released on Thursday by the independent geo-monitoring platform Nusantara Atlas, almost 2.88 million hectares of Indonesian territory was affected by fire from January to October 2026, rising nearly 1 million hectares in October alone.

The amount of fire-damaged land in the first three quarters of this year was 35% higher than in the same period of 2019, the last year Indonesia faced strong "super-El Nino" conditions, Nusantara Atlas said.
6ad98a1645c824ef: MELAKA, Nov 13 — Communications Minister Datuk Seri Fahmi Fadzil said that based on daily reports received from the National Cyber Security Agency (Nacsa), no particularly worrying cybersecurity incidents had been confirmed so far.
