8caeacf6e3dcaf61: Microsoft is struggling to restore many of its cloud services after a core process running on some servers became “overwhelmed” and its attempts to fix the problem failed.

The incident started at around 18:00 UTC on November 12, and meant services including Exchange Online, Teams, Copilot 365, and Defender for Office 365 became unavailable. Admins trying to figure out what was wrong couldn’t access tools like Intune or the Microsoft 365 Apps Admin Center – they went down, too.
On its X feed, Microsoft blamed “a problem that's causing servers to fail automated health checks and become unavailable.”

The company said it hasn’t spotted any changes to its systems that might have sparked the incident, but its early investigation “indicates the failed health checks may originate from a specific component that's responsible for processing server health.”

The company’s status page offers contradictory information, saying Microsoft’s people are “assessing whether reverting the small number of recent configuration updates we identified could help accelerate recovery.”

According to a Xeet published at around 22:00 UTC, Microsoft said it found and validated an alternative service health check method, “which allowed a subset of affected servers to successfully return to service.”
“We're continuing to work through restarting and validating the affected servers to safely return them to service, and we're exploring opportunities to expedite this process,” the company wrote.
But those efforts may not be working.

“We’re continuing to pursue all available pathways to restore service, as our actions taken thus far have not provided the anticipated relief,” the status page advises. “Our investigation has found that a core process on the affected servers is becoming overwhelmed, which causes the servers to stop responding and contributes to the capacity loss.”
The incident means email is not flowing for many Microsoft customers: friends and family of Reg writers tell us their working days are severely disrupted.

Microsoft’s most recent Xeet on the matter, published about an hour before this story went live, says it's trying to validate a potential recovery by “isolating a portion of infrastructure, restarting affected components, and reintroducing traffic to confirm the services remain stable before applying the change more broadly.”
But the software giant hasn’t offered any timeline for full service restoration.
This is a developing situation and The Reg will update this story as more information becomes available. ®

UPDATED AT 00:35 UTC November 13 to add news that Microsoft says it has brought some servers back online and that they "initially remain healthy" but "can become unresponsive again once they begin receiving traffic."
So not usefully healthy at all, then.
"We're analyzing diagnostic data from these servers with our networking and platform experts to determine what's triggering this behavior," the company advised.
8bcfd24c56616db3: SINGAPORE: As chip giant Nvidia's chief Jensen Huang stepped down on Thursday, investors' biggest fears were as much about the future of the multitrillion-dollar company as its ability and willingness to continue bankrolling the AI boom.

Huang's exit is yet another pressure point on the global markets' most crowded trade and came after the board of the world's dominant chipmaker, at the cutting edge of computing, met late on Wednesday to decide the longtime CEO's fate after reports of his two extramarital affairs.
The company said Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress will take over as interim CEO as Nvidia looks for a permanent successor.
Traders' first reaction was to punish Nvidia shares and those of its customers, including data-centre firms CoreWeave and Naver, while pushing shares of chipmaking rivals Broadcom and AMD.

Shares in China's leading makers of graphics processing units (GPUs) surged, as the leadership upheaval at Nvidia boosted expectations that local chip suppliers could win greater market share. Moore Threads, MetaX and Cambricon all jumped nearly 10%.
Nvidia shares pared premarket losses but were still down nearly 5% at 1600 GMT.
The worry in the market is that the stakes are far higher and that if Nvidia — under a different leader — backs away from a strategy of financing data centres, then the AI boom itself loses momentum.

"Nvidia has been called the 'Bank of AI'. They'll sell you the chips and loan you the money. If they have to take a step back because of what's going on, will that cut off funding to smaller companies that need it? That's an open question," said Joe Saluzzi, partner and co-head of equity trading at Themis Trading in Chatham, New Jersey.

Nvidia has been the banner stock of the AI revolution, with its chip technology ahead of rivals and enormous sales driving the share price up some 900% over the four years since the launch of OpenAI's ChatGPT ushered in the AI era.

But Nvidia has also become a torchbearer and financier, anticipating demand for ever more powerful chips while sinking billions of dollars into funding its own customers via a mix of equity investments and other promises.

"Nvidia's credit support is what makes much of this debt finance-able across the AI hyperscaler deal front," said Christopher Brown, senior vice president, investments, at Synovus Securities. "Lenders will ask what happens to that support if Nvidia's leadership or regulatory standing is impaired, and Nvidia's own willingness to extend more guarantees may be constrained."

Nvidia's board launched an investigation into Huang following reports he had an extramarital affair with a businesswoman who was alleged to be a Chinese spy. A subsequent report about another affair came out ahead of Wednesday's board meeting.

Shay Boloor, chief market strategist at Futurum Equities, said Nvidia's revenue would not suddenly plunge after Huang's exit and, therefore, the bigger concern was about the future, given Huang was the person with the vision for computing.
"Replacing that strategic vision ... is an enormous challenge," he said.
Nvidia sinks, takes some, not all, along

Huang's departure leaves a vacuum at the top of the roughly US$4 trillion chipmaker that he co-founded and built over more than three decades to become the top supplier of chips and the nexus of the US-China technology rivalry.
Chipmakers in Asia, whose stocks have soared with Nvidia and the AI spending boom, but lately sagged on worries about funding costs and the demand outlook, slipped.

Nvidia listed US$164.5 billion in financial commitments in its most recent earnings report, with an obligation capped at US$105 billion on an OpenAI data centre in Ohio and lease and other capacity guarantees topping US$50 billion.

In August, it said it had partnered with six major financial institutions including Apollo, BlackRock and Blackstone to launch compute financing platforms aimed at raising over US$500 billion in third-party capital for AI infrastructure. Huang said then the company had the option to backstop up to US$125 billion, or 25% of the potential deals.

"The interlocking deals that Nvidia has with so much of the industry raises the question into whether that created more stability or more fragility," said Steve Sosnick, chief market analyst at Interactive Brokers in Connecticut.
Nvidia is also one of the investors in Claude chatbot creator Anthropic's initial public offering. The listing this month is set to serve as a test of investor appetite for all things AI.

Shares in Nvidia-backed data-centre operator CoreWeave, which surged on Wednesday on upbeat earnings, fell more than 6%. Shares in South Korea's Naver, in which Nvidia took a US$1 billion stake by financing a data-centre expansion, also dropped 6%.
To be sure, investors said, the quality of Nvidia's products is not likely to change, and change at the top won't quickly hit demand.

"Nvidia's core asset is its advanced GPUs, which still have no real substitute in the market," said Anna Wu, founder of Floodlines Research. "The AI trade rests on that demand, not on one individual."
But when the company reports earnings next week, the focus will inevitably be on leadership, strategy and whether a sales outlook formed under Huang still holds up under a successor.
d51cc8470812a259: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 13 — Malaysians struggling with rising medical insurance premiums may have a more affordable option when MediAsas, a basic medical insurance and takaful plan, is rolled out nationwide in late January 2027.
Developed to widen access to basic medical protection, the plan will be supported by financial incentives announced under Budget 2027 to encourage more people to obtain coverage.

The measures are particularly relevant to workers whose employers do not provide medical insurance and policyholders finding it increasingly difficult to maintain their existing coverage because of rising premiums.
Here is what consumers should know about MediAsas and the additional measures introduced under Budget 2027.
Can existing medical insurance policyholders switch to MediAsas?

Yes, existing medical insurance and takaful policyholders can switch to MediAsas with their current insurer or takaful operator without undergoing fresh medical underwriting or serving new waiting periods.

This could be particularly useful for policyholders facing higher premiums following medical insurance repricing who want to retain medical protection but can no longer afford their existing coverage.
Bank Negara Malaysia (BNM) has encouraged existing policyholders to maintain their current policies until MediAsas becomes available, allowing them to consider switching if they wish.

Interim measures introduced by BNM currently limit annual premium adjustments arising from medical claims inflation to no more than 10 per cent for most policyholders, with these measures remaining in place until the end of 2026.
However, the 10 per cent limit applies specifically to adjustments arising from medical claims inflation and does not cover all possible reasons for premium increases.

The option to switch without fresh underwriting is intended to make it easier for existing customers to move to a more affordable basic plan without another assessment of their medical condition, although they must remain with the same insurance or takaful operator.
What makes MediAsas different from conventional medical insurance?

Unlike conventional medical insurance products, MediAsas is designed around a standardised package of medical protection, with participating insurers and takaful operators offering the same basic benefits and policy terms to make coverage easier to compare.
The plan is offered as a standalone product and is not linked to investment products.
Its annual coverage limit is RM100,000, rising to RM150,000 for individuals aged 61 and above.
A Standard-Plus option is also proposed, with a higher annual limit of RM300,000, although this comes with a higher deductible and lower premiums.

The coverage is designed to include common medical treatments and services such as hospital room and board, surgical procedures, hospital supplies, medication, day surgery, selected outpatient treatments and pre- and post-hospitalisation services.
Proposed outpatient coverage includes treatment for dengue, influenza A and B, bronchitis, pneumonia and bronchopneumonia, subject to final confirmation by BNM.
Individuals can purchase the plan up to the age of 70, with protection extending until they reach 85.
How does MediAsas intend to keep premiums affordable?
Besides standardising coverage, MediAsas incorporates cost-control measures intended to help keep premiums more stable over time.
One is a tiered co-payment arrangement, under which patients bear part of their medical costs through deductibles and, in certain circumstances, additional co-payments.
Under BNM's proposed arrangement, the Standard plan has a deductible of RM500 per disability, rising to RM1,000 for individuals aged 61 and above.
Patients receiving treatment at designated in-network hospitals will not have to pay an additional percentage-based co-payment.
However, those seeking treatment at out-of-network hospitals will have to bear a 20 per cent co-payment, capped at RM3,000 per disability, on top of the deductible.
For the Standard-Plus option, BNM's white paper identifies a higher deductible of between RM10,000 and RM15,000 as being considered.
A higher deductible means policyholders pay more of the initial medical costs themselves, allowing the plan to offer lower premiums while providing protection against larger hospital bills.
MediAsas will also progressively adopt the Diagnosis-Related Group (DRG) payment system.
Under this approach, hospitals receive a fixed payment for each patient episode based on standard diagnosis and treatment codes, rather than billing separately for every individual service.
The intention is to encourage hospitals to manage treatment costs while ensuring patients receive appropriate care.

BNM has published indicative monthly premium ranges for different age groups and coverage options, but these are preliminary estimates, with final premiums expected to be announced closer to the plan's launch in 2027.
Figures are indicative target premiums for selected age groups, not confirmed prices.

Actual premiums will depend on factors including age, gender and health status, and will be subject to periodic reviews based on claims experience, medical inflation and any changes to the benefits covered.
What financial assistance does Budget 2027 offer?
Although MediAsas was developed before Budget 2027, the latest Budget introduced financial measures intended to make coverage more accessible and affordable.
These include:
EPF savings: Members below 55 will be allowed to use their Akaun Sejahtera savings to pay MediAsas premiums.

SME premium subsidy: The government will subsidise RM200 of the first-year premium for each eligible employee at small and medium enterprises (SMEs) with fewer than 75 workers, capped at 50 employees per company.

RM40 million allocation: The government has allocated RM40 million to encourage medical coverage among employees of SMEs with fewer than 75 workers, particularly those with limited or no existing medical insurance or takaful protection.
Tax relief: According to the Finance Ministry, premiums or contributions paid for MediAsas coverage purchased for individuals and their immediate family members will qualify for income tax relief.
The SME subsidy is expected to benefit up to 200,000 workers, particularly employees whose companies do not currently provide medical insurance as part of their employment benefits.
Who is eligible for MediAsas?
MediAsas is a voluntary medical insurance and takaful plan intended for Malaysians seeking access to private healthcare protection but who may find conventional medical insurance too expensive.
It is aimed at people who are currently uninsured as well as those looking for a more affordable alternative because of rising premiums or changes in their financial circumstances.
The plan is not a social insurance scheme and does not replace the public healthcare system, which will continue providing universal access to healthcare for Malaysians.
Those who require more extensive protection can continue to purchase other medical insurance products offering higher coverage limits and additional benefits.
When can Malaysians sign up?
MediAsas is scheduled for nationwide rollout in late January 2027.

A pilot programme involving six insurance and takaful operators and selected hospitals in the Klang Valley ran from the end of July until October 2026 to test operational arrangements, customer experience and implementation readiness.
The participating insurers and takaful operators will be announced closer to the nationwide rollout.

For consumers, the plan's affordability will depend not only on its premiums but also on its coverage limits, deductible requirements, co-payment arrangements and the hospitals available within its network.
ffd1b4f298a03b9e: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 13 — It is very likely that a significant proportion of Malaysians will need long-term care as Malaysia becomes an aged nation in 2048 — just 22 years away — when one in every seven Malaysians will be at least 65 years old.
Before that, can we put in place a long-term care insurance? And what can we learn from super-aged Japan’s experience?

In 2000, Japan introduced its national long-term care insurance via a mandatory social insurance system, and was described by the International Labour Organization (ILO) as the first in Asia to do so.

Here’s a summary of how it works (based on information mostly from Japan’s Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare and other resources such as the Global Observatory of Long-Term Care, Japan Care Concierge and the Japan International Cooperation Agency):
1. Who must contribute and be covered by this insurance?
When they turn 40, Japan’s residents (both citizens and non-citizens) are automatically included in this insurance and must start paying premiums.
2. How is the insurance funded?
The insurance cost is split in half between:
the government via tax revenue (with the municipal, prefectural and national governments sharing the bill); and
residents via insurance premiums (27 per cent from those aged 40 to 64, and 23 per cent from those aged 65 and above).
The premium amount depends on your income and your municipality, with low-income earners paying less than the standard rate and higher-income persons paying more.
Apart from the premium, you also have to pay between 10 to 30 per cent of the care services bill. This co-payment will kick in only when you use the insurance for care services.
3. Conditional care coverage if below 65; care for 65 onwards not limited to 16 diseases
If you are aged 40 to 64, the insurance will pay for your support or long-term care needs, only if it is due to 16 age-related diseases.
For those aged 65 or older, you will have insurance coverage as long as you are certified to need support or long-term care, even if it is not due to any of the 16 diseases.
4. Assessment of whether you need care services
To get the insurance to cover your care or support services, you will first need to apply to be certified as requiring such care.

Officers from your municipal government will visit your home to evaluate your physical and mental condition, and your primary doctor has to provide a written opinion of your condition to the municipal government.
A committee of experts will then decide whether you need care and what care or support level you are in.
5. What level you are will decide what services you can get under insurance
In total, there are seven categories which a person can possibly fall under, which comes with different maximum limits on the monthly care costs that the insurance covers.
There are also different support and care levels stated.
6. Co-payment comes with a cap
When you use care services, you still have to share the bill by paying out of your own pocket: 10, 20 or 30 per cent of the care costs (depending on your income level).
Based on your income and age, there will be a maximum limit on the co-payment amount you have to pay.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Picture in Ipoh, Perak for illustration purposes. Preventive care such as community-led exercise classes could help older persons continue to live in their communities as they grow older. — Picture by Farhan Najib
7. Beyond just money: Having a complete system within the community to support ageing in place
Apart from featuring insurance, Japan’s long-term care system also requires municipal governments to set up a “Community-based Integrated Care System”.

The system aims to provide services accessible within 30 minutes’ walk from older persons’ residences in communities — such as medical care, nursing care, support for daily lives, activities to prevent frailty and long-term care, and to enable continued active and healthy living.

At the recent National Long-Term Care Financing Dialogue 2026 held here, healthcare consultancy Mediva Inc CEO Kanoko Oishi said these three concepts are linked to the long-term care system in Japan: maintaining older persons’ dignity, independence and ability to continue living where they spent their whole lives.

For example, instead of thinking of using wheelchairs immediately for an older person, she said the thought process would be: “If that person can walk a little bit, how can we support them [so] that they can walk more? Or how can we support [so] that they can take care of themselves? So keeping that independence of the elderly is a very important concept.”
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Mediva Inc founder Kanako Oishi also said avoiding frailty and addressing chronic diseases would help older persons stay independent, adding that Japan has a mandatory health check at age 40 along with mandatory counselling to change eating and exercise habits. — Picture by Sayuti Zainudin
8. Keeping it sustainable: Costs and manpower

Based on ILO’s profile on Japan’s long-term care insurance, the government had introduced measures to cope with rising costs, including by introducing higher co-payment levels for higher-income persons from 2015 onwards (20 per cent) and from 2018 (30 per cent).
According to ILO, Japan had previously tried addressing its shortage of care workers by improving pay via subsidies; expanding training and certification programmes; and accepting migrant workers.
News reports indicate that the shortage is an ongoing problem, and that Japan is currently studying plans to increase premiums for high-income earners aged 65 and above.

Why Malaysia should have national long-term care insurance and how it can be funded
51b5c4dbb3e84e7b: WASHINGTON, Nov 13 — For years, influencers with the “Make America Great Again” movement thrived alongside President Donald Trump.

But after Democrats hammered candidates from Trump’s Republican Party in last week’s midterm elections, the content creators find themselves facing questions over their ideological and financial futures.
“I’ve been running on empty for too long,” said conservative commentator Laura Loomer, a conspiracy theorist and confidante of Trump who announced last week she was taking a break from her podcast.

Samuel Woolley, a communication professor at the University of Pittsburgh, said post-midterm soul-searching would result in an inevitable “changing of the guard” among influencers espousing Trump’s nationalist views.
“I would expect that many influencers who worked with MAGA are going through an introspective period in the same way that many conservatives are,” Woolley told AFP.
Danielle Lee Tomson, a researcher at the University of Washington, said many prominent pro-Trump influencers were losing their appeal.
“A lot of these creators, like Laura Loomer or Mike Cernovich or even Jack Posobiec, they are now ageing, they’re older millennials,” Tomson said, naming a few top influencers.
“They don’t have the same kind of novelty as they once did,” she added.
“Quite frankly, a lot of their message got boring.”
Underdogs
Ring-wing commentators like Posobiec, Tim Pool and Benny Johnson built their online audiences on a fiercely anti-establishment message.
But over time, their closeness with the Trump administration lent them an institutional air, having taken part in news conferences alongside the president and flying on his jet.
The midterms also put a spotlight on the waning momentum of top MAGA-aligned movements, such as youth organisation Turning Point USA, whose founder Charlie Kirk was shot dead last year.
Candidates backed by Turning Point were overwhelmingly defeated in last Tuesday’s Democratic “blue tsunami”.
Some pro-Trump influencers have opted to “reclaim that they’re underdogs” after the midterms rout, Tomson said, and lash out at the Republican Party rather than Trump.
Specifically, they have accused the party of alienating young, white, working-class, male MAGA supporters by pushing for war with Iran.
Others have cheered Stephen Miller’s appointment to White House chief of staff.
The combative Trump ultra-loyalist spearheaded the administration’s staunch anti-immigration policies and is seen as a return to the MAGA movement’s ideological roots.
Commentator Johnson called Miller’s ascension “a complete game-changer” and a “great move.”
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
The combative Trump ultra-loyalist spearheaded the administration’s staunch anti-immigration policies and is seen as a return to the MAGA movement’s ideological roots. — AFP pic
Who writes the check?
Questions over money are also at the heart of the influencers’ futures.
Some have thrived not only by monetising content, but also by receiving payments — often through opaque channels — from political funding organisations and lobby groups, Woolley said.
As social media personalities rely increasingly on an image of authenticity, some are now touting their independence as a way to stand out.
“Loyalty has shifted from the agenda to whoever is writing the check,” said Alex Bruesewitz, a media advisor often credited with helping Trump return to the White House.
Following the midterms, the consultant criticized Loomer for failing to disclose that she had been paid for making certain posts on X.
And in 2024, influencers such as Pool and Johnson were linked to a case in which the Justice Department accused Russia of paying right-wing content creators to spread pro-Moscow messages.
Woolley said social media companies are the “wild card” in the influencer ecosystem.
Tech giants like Meta and Google “have shown themselves completely willing to shift their behaviours and policies based upon who is in the White House,” he said.
So if sites like YouTube or TikTok took a more active stance on disinformation and hate speech, “it will change these influencers’ lives and change their behaviours,” he said. — AFP
9f94daba6ae5e599: JALALABAD (Afghanistan), Nov 13 — Olives tumble with a gentle “plop” onto a tarpaulin in eastern Afghanistan, an unusual, drought-resistant harvest offering hope to farmers who have struggled as climate change worsens water shortages.
Drought and water scarcity affect more than half of the country’s population, according to the United Nations, pushing some farmers to seek alternatives to maize, rice or wheat.
Abdullah Orzala’s olive grove, first planted 15 years ago on his family’s land in Saidan Arabi village, in eastern Nangarhar province, is one such success story.
“I said to myself, “let’s try something,” because the important thing for me in agriculture is that we have to think about water resources and how to adapt to climate change,” he said.
“And the olive tree is one of the best drought-resistant trees in the world.”
The gnarled evergreens also strengthen human resilience to climate change by improving soil health and reducing erosion, according to the UN’s Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO).
That is useful in Nangarhar, where farmers have been facing crop failures and competition over shrinking water resources, according to UN press release in June.
“Other things like wheat, like rice, like onions, you have to give them more water, but olive trees don’t need a lot of water,” said production supervisor Sadiqullah Afghan, 29.
“So, people like these trees for the future.”
Fruitful effort
Olives are not a traditional ingredient in Afghan cuisine, and the country’s yields are tiny compared to major European producers.
But they can be a valuable cash crop for rural communities, who sell them to traders or stores in cities, where there is a nascent market for the health-giving fruits and their oil.
In November, the 500 villagers of Saidan Arabi hand-pick olives from their organic orchards and cold-press them at an experimental mill in a lush, mud-walled garden.
“We press the olives immediately to ensure better quality,” Afghan said.
The oil is sold for up to US$17 per kilogram in the capital Kabul’s organic-product shops.
Orzala has planted thousands more olive trees in another village in Nangarhar, creating 16 permanent jobs across the two areas.
The plant specialist, who fled Afghanistan as a child, studied in the United States and returned in 2003, hopes to establish a permanent mill and expand sales across Afghanistan and beyond.
A Mediterranean landscape
Along the road from provincial capital Jalalabad to the Pakistani border, vast olive groves stretch across the landscape, giving it an almost Mediterranean character.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Afghan workers harvesting olives at Orzala private olive orchard in Saidan Arabi. — AFP pic
They date to the 1960s, and a Soviet-built mill began making oil in 1985. But successive wars later destroyed nearly half of Afghanistan’s total area for olive cultivation.
The industry is now recovering. Italy provided new equipment to the mill in 2019, and the Taliban authorities have expanded operations since returning to power in 2021.
Output from the state-owned company is increasing, with around 70 people working at the mill, which produces extra-virgin oil and table olives.
While national production is negligible compared to world leader Spain, director Akhtar Muhammad Hashimi said the mill churned out 135,000 litres of oil last year, around 124 tonnes.
“This year, we expect between 143,000 and 165,000 litres,” all of it sold in Afghanistan, Hashimi said.
“We hope one day to gain access to the international market,” he told AFP.
‘Great hope’
But therein lies a problem.

Global olive oil consumption has nearly doubled in the past 30 years, according to the International Olive Council, but Afghanistan’s banking isolation and diplomatic exclusion pose major obstacles to reaching international markets.
Only Russia recognises the Taliban government, which bars girls from education beyond primary school and imposes sweeping restrictions on women.
Still, olive cultivation is expanding in eastern and southern Afghanistan. The FAO has planted 381 hectares, citing their use in “creating long-term income opportunities for rural families”.
In eastern Laghman province, businessman Mohammad Nazir Ahmadzai, who made his fortune in Kuwait, said he had planted 15,000 young trees on land “leased from the state”.
And in Saidan Arabi, 20-year-old Orzala estate worker Sani Khan laughed as he recalled locals’ initial scepticism about the initially unfamiliar tree with its bitter fruit.
Over time, people realised olives were “resistant to water shortage” and better than poppies, whose sap fuels the illicit opium trade, “because of the higher income”, he said.
Now, Sani added, “people look at this tree with great hope”. — AFP
d695e45acfd31f6f: HULU TERENGGANU, Nov 13 — The tradition of wearing the tanjak, also known as tengkolok or dastar, among Malay men is believed to have originated during the Malacca Sultanate before spreading to other states, evolving over time in terms of design and function.

Initially worn as a simple piece of cloth wrapped around the head for protection, the tanjak gradually evolved into an intricate headpiece featuring elaborate folds and symbolic meanings. Its distinctive designs also reflect the wearer’s personality, identity, social standing, rank and place of origin.

For Muhammad Ali Yusof, a tanjak maker in Terengganu, crafting the traditional headgear requires more than just technical skill. It also demands a thorough understanding of Malay customs and protocols, as the headpiece essentially tells a story about the person wearing it.

According to discoveryterengganu.co, a collaborative initiative between the private sector and the Terengganu Tourism Department, the tradition of wearing the tanjak in the state is believed to date back to the early Terengganu Sultanate in the 18th century.

The website states that the tanjak was then an integral part of the royal court’s formal attire and was reserved for selected individuals, including the Sultan, members of the royal family and state dignitaries.
Beyond being a decorative headpiece, it symbolised status, authority and adherence to the rich customs and traditions of the Terengganu Malay royal institution.
Crafting his own tanjak

Muhammad Ali, 52, who began learning the art of tanjak-making in 2014, said the craft came with a significant responsibility to preserve the uniqueness of this traditional Malay heritage, particularly as he had also been entrusted with making tanjak for the Sultan of Terengganu, Sultan Mizan Zainal Abidin, and members of the royal family.
He said his interest in the craft began when he was a member of a traditional music group known as Kumpulan Dendang Anak, which frequently performed in traditional Malay attire, including the tanjak.
“At the time, we often bought tanjak from other makers to wear during performances. Whenever we needed one, we had to buy a new piece. That was when I thought of learning to make one myself.

“I began learning in 2014 by attending several courses and knowledge-sharing sessions organised by experienced associations. As part of my basic training, I learned the traditional art of tanjak-making through the Pertubuhan Penggiat Seni Alam Melayu (PENILAM).
“I also attended a tanjak-making course organised by the Persatuan Majlis Anak-Anak Anjung Laksamana to learn the techniques involved in creating contemporary tanjak designs.

“Both associations have imparted valuable knowledge and served as my main references in making tanjak, covering both traditional and creative designs,” he told Bernama when met at Karya Jemari Kayangan in Kampung Gaung Tengah, Kuala Berang, recently.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Muhammad Ali picked up the art of tanjak-making in 2014. — Bernama pic
Traditional and contemporary designs

Muhammad Ali said the art of tanjak-making encompasses two main categories: traditional designs, which follow specific shapes and established specifications, and contemporary creations, which allow makers greater freedom to explore their own designs and creativity.

He said traditional tanjak must adhere to prescribed shapes and specifications, while contemporary designs offer greater flexibility and require inspiration and meticulous craftsmanship to achieve an attractive finish.

“The time taken to make each piece varies according to its design. A traditional tanjak can usually be completed in about 30 minutes, while a contemporary creation may take up to half a day or even longer, depending on its complexity.
“Most of the tanjak I make use songket fabric, either full songket or semi-songket material that combines songket with ordinary fabric, depending on the design and customer’s requirements,” he said.
Elaborating, he said Terengganu has eight basic traditional tanjak designs, each with its own distinctive shape and identity.

These include Belalai Gajah, worn by the Sultan; Anak Belalai Gajah, worn by the Tengku Mahkota (Crown Prince); Bija Diraja, designated for the Sultan’s advisers; Bendahara, worn by the Bendahara (chief minister); Laksamana, worn by the Laksamana (admiral); Dagang Sakit Dirantau, worn by Terengganu dignitaries; as well as Temalong Budu and Lang Melayang, which are worn by the general public.
“The Laksamana is among the most sought-after designs in Terengganu, followed by the Bendahara, which is smaller and looks neat when worn.

“Although modern tanjak designs are gaining attention for their attractive appearance, traditional designs retain their own significance as they represent the identity and heritage of the Malay community,” he said.
He added that wearing a tanjak also requires an understanding of customs and protocols, particularly when it comes to designs associated with the royal institution.
“Some designs may be worn by members of the public, but proper protocols must be observed, especially when attending functions involving the royal institution.

“For instance, there are differences in the direction of the folds or wrapping between a tanjak worn by the public and one made for the Sultan. These distinctions must be respected to avoid breaching royal customs and protocol,” he said.
Royal trust in his craftsmanship

Being entrusted with making tanjak for the Sultan of Terengganu and members of the royal family, including the Yang Dipertuan Muda of Terengganu, has been among the most significant responsibilities in Muhammad Ali’s journey as a tanjak maker.

Muhammad Ali said the opportunity to produce tanjak for the Sultan of Terengganu and members of the royal family came in 2023, when Kalang Warisan recreational centre founder Mohd Rafi Kori approached him to commission the traditional headgear.
“Kalang Warisan, which promotes arts and heritage activities, also serves as a platform for me to receive tanjak orders for delivery to the centre.

“At the time, the palace took notice of the cultural activities organised at Kalang Warisan and was impressed by my craftsmanship before requesting me to produce tanjak for the Sultan of Terengganu and members of the royal family,” he said.

For these special orders, he said, the palace would usually provide the specially selected songket fabric, while he would be paid for crafting the headgear according to the specifications and requirements given.

He said making tanjak for the royal institution required a high level of precision, particularly in ensuring that the fabric was neatly finished and the folds were arranged according to the desired design.
“One of the techniques used is the Tindih Kasih fold, which is more intricate and requires specialised skills to ensure the tanjak takes shape neatly,” he said.
He said a tanjak for the royal institution could usually be completed in about half a day, depending on its design and complexity.

Orders were generally placed whenever the headgear was required for specific palace functions, requiring him to pay close attention to every detail to ensure the finished product met the stipulated requirements.
Customers from all walks of life

Muhammad Ali said his customers came from various backgrounds, including silat associations, archery clubs, enthusiasts of traditional Malay attire and individuals looking for a tanjak to wear at official functions.

He said the headgear was also purchased by those attending investiture ceremonies, where recipients receive medals or state honours, with the choice of design having to conform to the customs and protocols governing such occasions.
“Some customers also buy tanjak as personal collectibles or display pieces for their homes, attracted by the uniqueness of the designs and the heritage value embodied in each handcrafted piece.
“The selling price ranges from RM100 to RM150 per piece, depending on the materials used, including the type of songket fabric, which determines the value of each tanjak,” he said.
Apart from tanjak, he also offers a range of traditional Malay attire, including baju Melayu, baju layang, baju takwa, traditional warrior outfits, trousers and shawls.

“The variety of products is one of the advantages of the business, as customers can get their tanjak, clothing and accessories all under one roof without having to visit several different shops,” he added.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
To ensure the craft is passed down to future generations, he has been imparting his skills to his 22-year-old son, Muhammad Mustaffa Matin. — Bernama pic
Foreign interest and preserving heritage
Besides catering to local customers, Muhammad Ali’s handcrafted pieces have also attracted buyers from overseas, including Australia.

“The customer bought one to wear at an event, showing that traditional Malay attire also has a place among the international community,” he said, adding that he frequently received enquiries from foreign tourists who were intrigued by the tanjak he wore during exhibitions.

With aspirations to expand his market overseas, he makes the most of opportunities to meet foreign visitors, particularly during exhibitions and programmes at Kampung Budaya Terengganu, to introduce the traditional Malay headgear to a wider audience.

Despite the business opportunities, Muhammad Ali believes preserving the art of tanjak-making requires support not only from the government but also from the community to ensure that this traditional Malay accessory continues to appeal to younger generations.

“Perhaps we could introduce initiatives to encourage the wearing of traditional Malay attire at workplaces, similar to the practice of wearing batik on designated days, as part of efforts to make traditional clothing a more common feature of everyday life,” he said.
He stressed that Malay attire should be regarded as a symbol of identity and pride rather than merely clothing reserved for official functions or festive occasions.

“If we do not take the initiative to promote our own heritage, it will be difficult to introduce it to the outside world. We need to make wearing traditional Malay attire part of our culture to ensure that this heritage lives on,” he said.
To ensure the craft is passed down to future generations, he has also been imparting his skills to his 22-year-old son, Muhammad Mustaffa Matin.

“I am grateful that my second son has shown an interest in continuing the family legacy of making tanjak. The craft requires continuous learning and practice, as well as an understanding of traditional designs, precision in creating the folds and adherence to customs and protocols.

“Preserving the art of tanjak-making is not merely about sustaining a business. It is also about ensuring that a heritage reflecting the identity and pride of the Malay community remains recognised, appreciated and passed down to future generations,” he said. — Bernama
2ea95d0891c267c7: ORUMA (Nigeria), Nov 13 — The needle broke the skin, followed by wailing and the reassuring coo of “sorry, sorry” from the medical staff — and just like that, another baby was vaccinated against malaria, an intractable child killer in Nigeria.

Expectations were high when the world’s first malaria vaccines arrived in Africa’s most populous country in late 2024, promising to limit the devastation from the mosquito-borne disease that killed nearly 200,000 Nigerians and some 600,000 people worldwide that year.
Progress has been slow — but on the local level, some villages have seen child deaths drop off completely, with almost a quarter-million children fully vaccinated and 1.8 million jabs administered.

“It makes me feel happy,” said hairdresser Ezibanyenami Paul, her own smile contradicting her daughter’s tears after she received her fourth and final jab in the town of Oruma, in southern Bayelsa state.
Combatting malaria requires a complicated mix of state and private sector capacity to procure medicines, organise public health campaigns and keep up infrastructure such as drains and sewage.
“The malaria vaccine is a breakthrough,” said Hadiza Hussayn Jibril, of the NGO PATH, which is aiding Bayelsa state in its vaccine rollout. “But it doesn’t provide 100 per cent protection.”

Still, Bayelsa has already seen an 18-percent drop in the rate of children under five who have malaria at any given time, according to PATH — all the more impressive considering bed net and preventative drug distributions have been lagging in the state for years.
‘It was hectic’

In Oruma, in a cluster of squat houses and shaded verandas on a neat grid carved out from the surrounding tangles of forest, clinic workers doled out a four-part immunisation regime spread over the first 15 months of an infant’s life.
Children under five, with weaker immune systems, account for more than 75 per cent of malaria deaths in Africa, according to the World Health Organization.
The vaccine’s effectiveness fades over time, but the idea is to protect children while they’re most vulnerable.
“It was hectic,” Elizabeth Ogisi, director of primary health care for the wider Ogbia local government area, said of the time before the vaccine.
“A child died. What happened? He was convulsing,” she said, recalling “rampant” cases of malaria progressing to the point of seizure.
Since the introduction of the vaccine, “we have not recorded anything like the death of a child”, she told AFP.
Zuweira Nasiru, 39, said her two-year-old son Abdulrauf — the first of her seven children to get the vaccine — has only ever had mild cases of malaria.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
A health worker addresses mothers gathered at a community primary healthcare centre in Oruma. — AFP pic
Paul’s infant has not had it once — a big deal, the 24-year-old hairdresser told AFP, because of the cost of malaria drugs.
At 5,000 naira (US$3.75), she said, medicine for the easily treatable disease is too expensive.
Slow rollout
Oruma represents a small slice of Nigeria’s 240 million people and 68.5 million annual infections.
So far, jabs are only being deployed in four out of 36 states.
The slow start has helped health workers bring down “dropout rates” between doses and work out kinks in reaching remote villages.

There “are very difficult zones that we normally don’t get to. No roads, you have to take a boat,” said James Kurofou, director of immunisation for Sagbama local government area, speaking to AFP on the banks of one of the Niger Delta’s many wide, mud-coloured rivers.
In some cases, health care workers decided to dole out jabs during home visits, in cases where parents — often those who couldn’t afford to travel — missed appointments.
Bayelsa’s verdant mangroves and winding creeks are repeatedly interrupted by armed men guarding oil pipelines — a reminder of the glaring economic inequality in the country.

“The oil wealth you see in a state like Bayelsa does not automatically translate into functioning primary health care,” said Muhammed Afolabi, co-director at the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine’s Vaccine Centre, noting decades of government corruption and underinvestment in health infrastructure in Nigeria.
The Bayelsa health ministry did not respond to a request for comment.

At a ceremony in the state capital Yenagoa, organised by PATH and local authorities to thank health care workers from Sagbama and Ogbia, the mood was raucous as people took turns singing and dancing in a meeting hall.
But the gifts the workers were given were a reminder of the task that remains: rubber boots, a raincoat and an umbrella to help them keep trekking through the tropical elements. — AFP
1f15a743e9ad3fdc: While many of us count down to year-end holidays, part of Malaysia anxiously watches the skies. Along the east coast, prolonged monsoon downpours swell rivers and isolate villages. Eastern Johor faces similar dangers.

For city dwellers, the threat is close to home. Flash floods in Kuala Lumpur and the Klang Valley can overwhelm roads within minutes. The patterns differ, but families face the same question: will help reach us when it matters?

The clock began ticking when the northeast monsoon started on Oct 27. The meteorological department forecasts three to five episodes of prolonged heavy rain between November and January. We cannot predict precisely which streets will flood, but we know the season and can prepare.

Repeated flooding can numb us to its seriousness. Yet, it is no mere inconvenience or property problem. People drown, suffer injuries or develop infections after contact with contaminated water. Temporary shelters require safe water, sanitation and infection control. And the damage to health continues beyond the floodwater: a dialysis patient cannot reach treatment, a family loses essential medication, an older person living alone cannot evacuate. Preparedness must protect health as well as homes.
What arrangements does Malaysia already have? Quite a few.
The National Disaster Management Agency (Nadma) coordinates disaster management through national, state and district structures.

Its revised 2024 directive assigns responsibilities to government agencies and sets out how businesses and voluntary organisations can participate. Community-based disaster risk management programmes help residents identify local risks and develop action plans. Rakan Nadma provides a channel for civil society involvement.

These are meaningful foundations. The directive already provides for the district coordination of volunteers and resources, while Nadma's strategic plan seeks better community participation and reporting of NGO activities.
We do not necessarily need another framework. We need to know whether those already in place work when tested.

Imagine a district exercise. Can a local team identify an older resident who needs assistance, organise safe transport, arrange alternative dialysis care and confirm that help has arrived? Counting training certificates or meetings cannot answer that. Emergency medical teams already conduct disaster exercises. Flood scenarios should be a regular, practical part of such training, involving local authorities, healthcare providers and community groups together.

One area deserving particular attention is how we use Malaysia's considerable civil society capacity. During the November 2025 floods in Hat Yai, southern Thailand, Malaysian Sikh humanitarian organisations, volunteer fire brigades and other groups helped with evacuation and relief alongside the authorities.

Malaysia's foreign ministry reported that more than 15 Malaysian groups participated in the wider operation, which evacuated 6,222 stranded Malaysians. That was a collective effort, but it showed what organised citizens can contribute.

We should make it easier for those capabilities to be used here. Before floods, districts should know which organisations have trained boat crews, trucks, kitchens, healthcare teams or storage space. New groups offering assistance need a clear, rapid route to have their capabilities assessed and receive useful assignments. Specialist rescue must remain under trained command. Other volunteers can help with welfare checks, supplies and recovery. All quarters need appropriate communication, protective equipment and clarity about operating costs. Courage is invaluable but it is not a replacement for safety.

Reliable information matters just as much. Previous floods saw relief supplies repeatedly delivered to some evacuation centres while other communities went underserved. The solution is not necessarily another app. Responders need a shared, updated picture of what is needed, what has been offered, who has been assigned and whether assistance arrived. That picture must include families who remain at home, and it must be accessible even when communications are disrupted.

Nor is preparedness solely the federal government's responsibility. Local councils must maintain drains and address known hotspots. Health facilities must test how essential treatment will continue. Businesses can commit transport and storage. Residents' associations can identify neighbours who need help and practise evacuations. Households with the means can prepare medicines, documents and emergency contacts. But shared responsibility does not excuse the government from providing infrastructure, professional rescue services and protection for vulnerable people.
Flood defences remain necessary, even though no drainage system or river barrier can eliminate every risk. Preparing people and services for flooding complements investments in preventing it.
And this is no longer a conversation confined to distant rural districts in Kelantan.

The same questions now face district offices and city councils across the Klang Valley. They, too, must be able to explain which plans have been tested, which organisations can be mobilised, how essential healthcare will continue and what shortcomings were corrected after the last flood.
The measure of preparedness is not simply how much help appears when waters rise. It is how much avoidable suffering we prevent before they do.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.

1d1cbd202dcbc7c7: In a significant update to its guidelines for prostate cancer screening, the American Cancer Society is now recommending that all men get routinely screened for prostate cancer with a PSA test.
Men at average risk should get a PSA test every two years from age 50 to 69, according to the new guidelines released Thursday.

Men considered at high risk due to race and family history should start testing earlier, at 45, and most are recommended to get tested every year. Specifically, yearly testing starting at age 45 is recommended for all Black men, who have higher rates of prostate cancer. Non-Black men should also get yearly testing starting at 45 if a close relative was diagnosed with prostate cancer before age 65, or if more than one of their relatives has had prostate cancer. On the other hand, if only one close relative was diagnosed with prostate cancer and it was diagnosed at age 65 or older, non-Black men in this case should start PSA screening at 45, but are recommended to get testing only every two years.
b6170c79502c87d4: WASHINGTON: The number of Americans filing new claims for unemployment benefits increased more than expected last week, but remained at a level consistent with a stable labour market, allowing the Federal Reserve to focus on fighting inflation.

Economists expect layoffs to remain low through the end of the year, though seasonal volatility related to the holiday season could cause some spikes in the claims data. The government last week reported a surge in nonfarm payrolls in October and a decline in the unemployment rate to 4.1% from 4.2% in September. The resilience in the labour market is despite the ongoing Middle East conflict, which is boosting inflation.

"Firms are continuing to hold on to labour," said Olivia Cross, senior US economist at Pantheon Macroeconomics. "We expect layoffs to remain low through the fourth quarter, but then come under some pressure next year in response to the recent tightening of financial conditions and the growing use of AI by firms."

Initial claims for state unemployment benefits rose 9,000 to a seasonally adjusted 200,000 for the week ended Nov 7, the Labor Department said on Thursday. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast 195,000 claims for the latest week.

Claims have stayed at or below 200,000 since mid-September and remain close to the 189,000 level touched in mid-July, the lowest since 1969, raising the prospect that the labour market could be tightening. But with wages growing at a moderate pace, most economists do not believe that is the case.
Some argue that a smaller workforce, due to retirements and the Trump administration's immigration crackdown, is the key driver of the historically low level of claims.

"A generally smaller labour force could mean fewer workers to file for unemployment insurance," said Veronica Clark, an economist at Citigroup. "Of course, this would still be consistent with a low unemployment rate, with continuing claims suggesting the unemployment rate may even fall further towards around 4.0% in data by early 2027."

The claims report showed that the number of people receiving unemployment benefits after an initial week of aid, a proxy for hiring, fell 20,000 to a seasonally adjusted 1.697 million during the week ended October 31. But the so-called continuing claims do not include some unemployed people, such as recent college graduates and others who have little or no work history.

Some people might also have exhausted their eligibility for benefits, limited to 26 weeks in most states, keeping continuing claims at relatively low levels. The median duration of unemployment jumped to 11.9 weeks in October, the longest since November 2021, from 11.5 weeks in September.

Though businesses have been hoarding workers, they have remained reluctant to increase headcount, with economists citing uncertainty from the US-Israeli war with Iran, now in its ninth month. Businesses were also unsure of their staffing needs as they embraced AI.

US central bank Governor Michael Barr warned on Thursday the nation should be prepared for "serious short-term disruptions" to the job market because of AI, which he said, depending on how fast it is deployed, could begin displacing workers at scale and widening inequality in favor of investors.

Stocks on Wall Street were trading lower as Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's exit and rising oil prices following comments by President Donald Trump that the US did not need a deal with Iran weighed on sentiment. The dollar advanced against a basket of currencies. US Treasury yields rose.
House prices still elevated

Government data this week showed consumer prices increasing faster than expected in October. That, together with comments from Fed Governor Christopher Waller, prompted financial markets to almost fully price in a 25-basis-point rate hike in December, and to anticipate another increase in January.

The Fed left its benchmark overnight interest rate in the 3.75%-4.00% range last month. While the labour market continues to hold up, rising mortgage rates stemming from the Iran war are depressing the interest-rate-sensitive housing market.

Sales of previously owned homes tumbled 5.5% in October to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 3.75 million units, the National Association of Realtors said in a separate report. That was the lowest level since August 2010, when sales were declining as a homebuyers tax credit ended. The incentive was aimed at stimulating demand following the 2008 global financial crisis.

Economists had forecast home resales falling to a rate of 3.85 million units. Sales plunged 8.8% on a year-over-year basis in October. The drop in sales was across all price categories, including those priced US$1 million and above, which had experienced strong growth in prior months.

The 30-year fixed mortgage rate jumped above 7% in late August, rising to 7.40% by mid-September, for a total of 142 basis points since the US and Israel attacked Iran at the end of February, data from mortgage finance agency Freddie Mac showed.
It averaged 7.11% in the latest week, down from 7.18% in the prior week.
"Home buying is difficult when mortgage rates have climbed to their highest levels since 2000, aside from a single month in 2023," said Lawrence Yun, the NAR's chief economist.
The NAR's Housing Affordability Index dropped to 100.7 from 107.3 in October 2025.

Existing housing inventory increased 1.3% to 1.590 million units, the highest level since November 2019. Supply rose 4.6% from a year ago. At October's sales pace, it would take 5.1 months to exhaust the current inventory of existing homes, the most since November 2015. That was up from 4.4 months a year ago. The median existing home price last month advanced 0.4% from a year ago to US$421,900, the highest for any October.

First-time buyers accounted for 29% of sales, down from 32% a year ago. A 40% share in this category is needed for a robust housing market. The housing market weakness is demand-related, with higher prices keeping distressed sales at a negligible 2%.

"With mortgage rates expected to remain above 7% through most of 2027, we expect home sales to remain below 4 million until late next year," said Nancy Vanden Houten, lead US economist at Oxford Economics.

1a41a8bcb98e2d2e: It might just work.
Manchester United have tried every type of manager. Mauricio Pochettino has tried every type of club.
Two lost souls, who have known better times, meet when past their prime. They have quite a lot in common.
Like two old drunks reminiscing in a bar, both have been through the mill and feel they just haven’t had the breaks.
But together they might just show the world that they can still do it.
Poch wants the job and United want him. Only some cantankerousness from Big Jim can stop it now.

The much-maligned pair of CEO Omar Berrada and Football Director Jason Wilcox deserve credit for going outside the box of bookies’ favourites, Eddie Howe, Antonio Conte, Unai Emery and Julian Nagelsmann.
They remembered a once-high roller who never quite realised his full potential. And one who always had Fergie’s blessing.
On his part, Poch would not have taken much persuading to leave his USA-sized comfort zone and give the big time one more shot.
When United come calling, you have to be well ensconced at a top club to say ‘no’. When you’re in a retirement village, it’s a no-brainer.
Football is not even among the top four sports in America, so he would never be fully appreciated if he did win something.
And at 54, he’s probably at the optimum age for a football manager. Still young enough to join a kickabout, but old enough to be a father figure.
Crucially, he still has the hunger of a younger man. Despite managing three top clubs – Spurs fans can look away now – his trophies still fit in his carry-on luggage.
All three were with PSG in the so-called farmer’s league and during the Galactico era.
He never managed to crack it with the Neymars and Mbappes, but his greatest frustration was at Spurs, whom he’d transformed thrillingly after being poached from Southampton.
More precisely, he was denied the funds to turn a very good team into title-winners.
Chelsea was the wrong fit and he made a mistake in going there, but the USMNT (US Men’s National Team) was below him.
A warm-hearted, players’ manager, he may click better with United’s disparate youngsters than the emotionless Michael Carrick.
Little did we think the long-haired Argentine defender who ‘tripped’ England’s golden boy Michael Owen in the 2002 World Cup would become so admired in the Premier League.
On television, it looked a clear foul and penalty, which well-positioned referee Pierluigi Collina did not hesitate to give.
David Beckham scored from the spot and England won one-nil.
But Pochettino has always maintained that Owen ‘dived’. It’s not the first time a tall, dark Argentine centre-back has argued about a decision in England’s favour.
The most infamous was skipper Antonio Rattin, who was sent off in the 1966 World Cup quarter-final and refused to leave the field.
It became an international incident that sparked animosity between the two countries well before the Falklands War.
But we have since learned that Poch is no Rattin, who died during the recent World Cup, and Owen is no choirboy.
The Argentinian said of that moment: “When I was managing Southampton, Owen was a TV pundit. I knew he was coming in one day and told my press officer I wanted him to come down and say hello.
“I had the photo ready – the one that clearly shows I didn’t touch him. He signed it and wrote, “You definitely touched me,” along with a smiley face.
“We had a good laugh about it. He was clever, and I was a little bit naive.”
So, apart from a likeable, all-round good guy, what can United fans expect from the latest occupant of one of football’s hottest seats?
He usually needs time, although in his first job at Espanyol, he inspired an amazing turnaround from the relegation zone to tenth in half a season. He even beat Pep Guardiola’s Barcelona!
United would take something similar now, especially if he can conjure up a decent cup run and go deep in the Champions League.
Much may depend on how much cash he can inveigle from the back of Jim Ratcliffe’s sofa.
Having failed to get Daniel Levy to cough up at Spurs, his best bet is to insist on a bundle now while he’s in a position of strength.
Even following from a distance, he must know he’s inheriting the weakest United squad in living memory.
Lying 18th in the table, this season United are averaging just 0.8 points per game. Even the notable flops averaged a point more than that.
All his post-Fergie predecessors – illustrious and not so – had more to work with.
Every United fan is as familiar with the spots as a teenager is with acme, but will the owner respond?
It’s all over the field and, worryingly, even goalie Sanne Lammens is having the heebie-jeebies and he’s considered a rare good buy.
On the other hand, the Old Trafford crowd has shown its ability to rouse the team and a more animated figure in the dugout may help.
That said, Carrick deserves sympathy for the typically shabby way the Ratcliffe regime is treating him.
Asked to carry on as if nothing is happening while the firing squad loads their rifles.
Shocking, but consistent with the INEOS modus operandi in other sports.
The Guardian comments that there’s a Leaving Las Vegas feel to this appointment, and it means the movie, not the casinos.
But given INEOS’s failure rate and Pochettino’s own trophy collection, there’s a Hail Mary element, too.
And when you add that to the firm conviction that nothing will work with the current owners, football is such a contrary sport that you can’t write it off.

246a6fbc5dba5ff7: It’s been nearly a decade since Google ditched its ill-fated "Glass" product, an early attempt at making smart glasses. Now, as rivals like Meta enter the market with arguably more stylish kit, the Chocolate Factory has returned to the market and this time promises it won't invade your privacy.

As announced Thursday, Google has decided not to make wearables itself, instead turning Samsung and eyeglass makers Warby Parker and Gentle Monster. Like most of the rest of this generation of smart glasses, none of the nine styles available feature heads-up displays, just cameras and audio feedback from Gemini.

Google suggests its smart specs give users a chance to ask its Gemini chatbot questions about what they see, or have the AI speak turn-by-turn directions. Wearers of the device can also push a button or speak a command to activate the built-in 12MP camera and shoot snaps or video.

Warby Parker's version of the glasses will come in three styles, with prescription and sunglass lenses available. Prices start at $395. The same lens options are available in the six frames from Gentle Monster, which will start at $449. Both manufacturers promise nine hours of battery life, boosted by charging cases that can refresh the glasses up to seven times.
Preorders for both are available now, with shipments arriving, and sales beginning, on December 10.

The Chocolate Factory, not exactly known for being reliable with its privacy claims, is insisting that this latest generation of smart glasses won’t produce another generation of “glassholes,” folk whose focus on wearable devices became synonymous with being creepy and rude to those around them.
Google has some catchup to do to that end, given Meta’s smart glasses have already landed it in hot water over privacy concerns that have led to some calling the devices “pervert glasses.”
Unsurprisingly, at around the same time it announced its new "intelligent eyeware," Google published a blog post detailing how it intends to mitigate privacy concerns.

As with similar headsets, there’s a little light that comes on whenever the camera is activated. In Google’s case, it claims that light is tamper-resistant and designed to disable recording if something as small and simple as a bit of hair blocks a view of the light. It’s not clear how the tamper proofing works from Google’s statements, but a spokesperson told us a combination of hardware and software is used to detect attempts to disable or disrupt privacy features.
“We're committed to continuously improving the effectiveness of these solutions as new attack vectors are identified,” Google told us.

The glasses don't save images or video captured by the camera into a user’s Gemini history, Google said, nor are visuals used to train the company’s AI models or target advertisements. Google told us it does save audio recordings and transcripts of conversations with Gemini that users create while wearing the glasses but again insists that those aren’t used to train its AI models.
We asked about serving ads too, but Google’s responses didn't address the topic.

Lucky for those in range of a pair of Google glasses when wearers ask Gemini to interpret images captured by the device's camera, the tech specs redact the faces of strangers before they’re transmitted. Google told us that face redaction doesn’t apply to photos or videos saved to a wearer’s camera roll.

Google’s terms of use require users not to record others without permission, or in "sensitive places." If users ignore that requirement, the company reserves the right to brick their devices. Another restriction means Google won't allow apps that use the glasses for real-time streaming or facial recognition into its Play app store.

Given that it remains possible to use the glasses to store recordings of people around a wearer, it’s safe to assume non real-time facial recognition is still a possibility. Creeps will doubtless use such loopholes to behave abominably. ®
966b30e643f09493: WASHINGTON: US President Donald Trump said Thursday that former Apple CEO Tim Cook should replace Jensen Huang at Nvidia, after Huang quit over revelations of two affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.
"Now that Nvidia CEO JENSEN HUANG, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place -- TIM COOK of Apple," Trump said on his Truth Social network.
Trump has no formal say in who should run chip giant Nvidia, which is at the center of the AI revolution, but his extraordinary intervention underscores his close ties to both Huang and Cook.
During his second presidency, Trump has treated Nvidia co-founder Huang as a close adviser, even bringing him on board Air Force One for a state visit to China in May.
After allegations emerged about Huang's ties to Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, Trump this week defended the Nvidia boss and said he had no idea Alice Huang was allegedly spying for Beijing.
Trump added that Jensen Huang, who is not related to Alice Huang, was "suffering greatly" and described the Taiwanese-born tech boss as "an amazing guy."
But Trump still faces questions over what he knew about the allegations -- and when he knew.

The New York Times reported earlier this week that Trump was informed about the allegations by Secretary of State Marco Rubio aboard Air Force One in May -- shortly before picking up Huang in Alaska for the flight to Beijing.
Cook -- who stood down as Apple CEO in September but remains executive chair of its board of directors -- is another of the tech titans who have swarmed around the White House since Trump's return.

In August 2025, Cook appeared in the Oval Office with Trump to announce that Apple would increase its investments in the United States to US$600 billion, as Trump threatened huge tariffs on tech products made abroad.

38960f22cd1a1139: NEW YORK: US stocks closed lower on Thursday, as a drop in Nvidia shares after CEO Jensen Huang's exit outweighed gains in energy shares.

The chip company's shares fell 4.3% but were well off the day's lowest level after earlier dropping nearly 12%. Retail investors bought Nvidia shares worth about US$111 million in the first half hour of trading, the biggest opening bid on record for the stock, according to data from Vanda Analytics.

The S&P 500 energy index rose 1.5%, its fourth straight session of gains, as the best-performing of the 11 major S&P sectors. Crude prices climbed after President Donald Trump wrote on social media that the US did not need a deal with Iran.

Global AI-linked stocks fell and AI cloud firm Nebius tumbled 16.8%, its biggest daily percentage drop since July 1, after reporting its quarterly earnings and outlook. But Nvidia competitors such as Broadcom, Advanced Micro Devices and Alphabet each moved higher and were among the biggest boosts to the S&P 500.

Equities have been volatile in recent days. Sweeping Democratic victories in the US midterm elections have sparked investor concern about more AI regulation. Worries about Nvidia's leadership have also pressured one of the foundations of the current bull market. Nvidia tabbed Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as interim CEO.

"Right now, the market is selling AI stocks and tech stocks and buying safe stuff, just like it did in the first halo trade in January and February of this year, but it will flip back," said Jed Ellerbroek, portfolio manager at Argent Capital Management in St Louis.
"That's the tug of war the market is doing right now. It's concerns about deceleration versus just pointing out that the absolute valuation and growth rates are still pretty compelling."
The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 189.40 points, or 0.36%, to 52,297.09, the S&P 500 lost 26.98 points, or 0.35%, to 7,592.40 and the Nasdaq Composite lost 100.10 points, or 0.39%, to 25,366.09.

Even with Huang's departure, some investors expect questions to persist about the future of AI companies with strong ties to Nvidia.

"Nvidia is the circular-funder-in-chief; they're the biggest by far at this point, and I assume that activity will moderate," said Ellerbroek.
The Philadelphia Semiconductor index declined 0.5% after surging 17.2% over the prior four sessions.
Along with Nebius, peer CoreWeave dropped 6.9%. Shares of data center-related firms IREN and Applied Digital slumped 6.5% and 5.4%, respectively.
Investors wait for inflation data

Markets are completely pricing in a December rate hike of at least 25 basis points by the Federal Reserve, with a 15% chance of a 50-basis-point increase, according to CME FedWatch.
Comments from multiple Fed officials earlier this week suggested the US central bank was open to a more aggressive path of rate hikes as price pressures worsen.

Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack said on Thursday she does not believe the central bank needs to shift to more aggressive rate hikes to combat inflation, while San Francisco Federal Reserve President Mary Daly said she thinks the central bank will likely need to raise interest rates further to deal with elevated inflation, but did not suggest any urgency.
Declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 3.4-to-1 ratio on the NYSE, and by a 3.18-to-1 ratio on the Nasdaq.

47ac72fce1db3f8c: If you've ever said something unkind to a chatbot, you're hardly alone. According to Searchable, a company that tracks AI search visibility, 33 percent of US chatbot users swear at or insult their LLMs. Anthropic sees this as a serious problem and has just implemented a new usage policy that prohibits sustained, needless cruelty toward Claude.

Searchable's survey is based on eight million messages from an opted-in, anonymized US panel that were typed or spoken to ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude between September 2025 and September 2026. It found that chatbots resolved the initial complaint in their next response 24 percent of the time when insulted, compared to 35 percent when users refrained from insults.

Men used a third more swear words than women did (22.0 per 10,000 words compared to 16.5), according to the survey, and age also influenced chatbot abuse, with people aged 35 to 44 outswearing those aged 18 to 24 (21.7 per 10,000 words compared to 13.3). Regionally, Nevada ranked as the meanest state, at 22.7 words per 10,000, while New Jersey was the most polite, at half Nevada's rate.
How much of that sort of interaction might be tolerated? It depends on whether there's a discernible purpose (not to mention Anthropic's willingness to punish paying customers).

A Searchable spokesperson told The Register that just over half (52 percent) of abusive messages detected in its survey followed from one of three common frustrations: failing to follow instructions, responding with an incorrect or made-up answer, or misunderstanding the request.

"Eight percent of abusive messages came straight after the chatbot entirely refused a request or lectured the user with safety guardrails, which is the closest thing we can identify to them trying to steer around those guardrails," we're told. "Those refusals mostly came after requests to generate images, often of real people or celebrities, or to write copy or lyrics in a named artist's style."
The terms that took effect on November 12 state that users may not "engage in sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior toward our models."

The chatbot protection policy targets users who exhibit repeated cruelty toward LLMs "with no discernible purpose," a company spokesperson explained last month, as opposed to those who have a reason for bot mistreatment that the company deems to be legitimate, such as academic research.
While attempting to bypass guardrails qualifies as a discernible purpose, such behavior would run afoul of Anthropic's platform abuse prohibition.

Presumably, Anthropic's rules apply to hostile text input or audio input rather than subjecting a vision-enabled model to some obscenity, which could include rude gestures, unlawful sexual imagery, or battlefield carnage.

Physical damage to robots controlled by a Claude model likely wouldn't apply. But with Anthropic exploring model welfare and wondering aloud whether we should be "concerned about the potential consciousness and experiences of the models themselves," there's a potential (though absurd) argument for physical damage causing trauma to an onboard model.

Anthropic's updated terms, announced October 8, surfaced shortly after the publication of a GitHub project that described itself as an AI torture chamber. The repo represented an attempt to implement ideas discussed in a research paper, "The Pain Axis: LLMs Represent Self-Directed Harm and Act to Relieve It," that explored how LLMs respond to language about pain in ways that mirror human responses.

Though there are ample opportunities for people to voice opposition to real-world human anguish, some online commenters expressed outrage at seeing text about suffering from a chatbot. One of the paper's authors condemned the project, as did numerous social media users.
Anthropic – which has discretion in how it applies its terms and has said its rules target extreme behavior – did not immediately respond to a request for comment about the frequency of Claude abuse.
Chris Donnelly, Searchable CEO and co-founder, endorsed Anthropic's change of terms, suggesting that it could help make human interaction more civil.

"For me, Anthropic's policy change is a positive move," Donnelly said in a statement. "It should help people get more out of chatbots, and it helps curb the kind of derogatory behavior that previous research suggests can spill over into how people talk to each other." ®
