45bb36293003f958: Hackers have used a dodgy third-party ScreenConnect extension to push malware onto at least 288 machines across 48 organizations, prompting ConnectWise to disable a handful of plugins in hundreds of customer environments.

Security outfit Huntress first raised the alarm in a Reddit post on Wednesday, warning of an active campaign targeting cloud-hosted ScreenConnect instances. At the time, its security operations center was tracking six compromised managed service providers (MSPs) and more than 286 affected endpoints, with the numbers still climbing.
ConnectWise acquired popular remote supporttool ScreenConnect in February, 2015.

Huntress spotted the attacks at around 1747 UTC, when someone began using ScreenConnect's remote command feature to install rogue clients on machines managed by multiple IT service providers. All 288 endpoints were hit within 90 minutes, with roughly a third compromised in the first ten minutes.
Huntress suspects more MSPs may have been compromised, as the attackers appeared to be numbering their victims sequentially, with the numbers suggesting earlier attacks that it hadn't detected.

The attackers deployed a 16-file malware toolkit dubbed SCKit, which installs a separate ScreenConnect client to maintain remote access even if the legitimate connection is shut down. It also contains code designed to spread the infection to IT technicians and potentially other customers under their control.

Huntress has since traced the activity to a possible authentication weakness in RMM+, a third-party extension that lets other management tools issue commands through ScreenConnect without technicians using its console.

Versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32 of the extension contain a flaw that means installations without a configured access key will accept a blank one. Because RMM+ operates independently of ScreenConnect's normal user accounts and authentication controls, an attacker could potentially execute commands without defeating MFA.
Huntress said the findings matched what its investigators saw during the attacks, with commands reaching machines across several ScreenConnect installations despite no corresponding login activity.
The researchers also confirmed that the attacks affected ScreenConnect versions 26.6.6.9747 and 26.7.6.9783, meaning administrators running the latest releases weren't necessarily safe.
ConnectWise has acknowledged that third-party extensions may have been involved but has stopped short of confirming how the attackers initially gained access.

In a security advisory, the company said it was investigating unauthorized access to certain partner environments and had identified approximately 400 installations containing at least one extension from the RMM+ family.
It has disabled five extensions, including RMM+, RMM Plus, and Labtech Plus, wherever it can do so remotely, and urged customers running their own ScreenConnect servers to follow suit.
ConnectWise stressed that the 400 environments were identified because they had the extensions installed, not because they were necessarily compromised.
The company said: "At this time, we have found no evidence of a compromise of ConnectWise infrastructure or a vulnerability in ScreenConnect itself."

There's another nasty trick buried in SCKit. According to Huntress, the malware is designed to turn an infected computer into a trap for the technician sent to investigate it. If the technician connects through ScreenConnect, the toolkit attempts to transfer malware back to their workstation, steal authentication cookies, and use their access to infect other machines.
That could give attackers a route from one compromised customer into others managed by the same IT provider. However, Huntress says it has yet to see that part of the attack succeed.
"We have not observed that method to spread work successfully. The console-takeover attempt failed in every recovered host log we have checked so far," the researchers wrote.

Huntress also suspects that some of the malware's C# code was generated using an LLM, pointing to unusually detailed comments explaining what the code is supposed to do. Apparently, even malware authors appreciate a little help with their homework.

Both Huntress and ConnectWise are urging administrators not to investigate suspected infections by remotely connecting through ScreenConnect, since doing so could put the technician's own machine at risk.

Administrators are being advised to use other security tools to investigate affected machines, look for rogue ScreenConnect clients, and check what commands have been run. Any malware left behind will also need to be removed before the machines are brought back online.
Huntress warned on Reddit that some machines were becoming reinfected within minutes of being taken out of isolation because the malware had not been properly removed.

Simply disabling the vulnerable extensions won't necessarily undo the damage, either. As ConnectWise warns, "Disabling extensions and resetting credentials alone may not remove unauthorized software, persistence mechanisms, or access already established on endpoints."
And with the attackers already able to install their own remote access software, kicking them out could prove considerably harder than closing the door they came through. ®

bc866c4bf647ff68: MANILA, Nov 12 — Global leaders are set to descend on Asia for a series of high-stakes meetings that will tackle everything from AI to trade to, potentially, nuclear disarmament.
AFP looks at a few of the key issues to watch for in the days ahead:
Three summits, five days

The 11-nation Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) opens its final leaders’ summit of the year on Sunday in Manila, while French President Emmanuel Macron attends a Francophonie summit in Phnom Penh.
Focus then shifts north for the annual Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) conference in Shenzhen.
Russian President Vladimir Putin is expected to be a key figure at Apec, while India’s Narendra Modi will be attending the Asean meet.
US President Donald Trump and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney will travel to both.
Analysts told AFP that the bruising midterm election defeat Trump recently suffered will not appreciably change how the US president is perceived.
“I don’t think the region will see him as a lame duck,” Siew Mun Tang, former head of the Asean Studies Centre at Singapore’s Iseas-Yusof Ishak Institute, told AFP.
“He has two more years. He can do a lot of things.”
Xi-Trump-Putin meet
The agenda for a proposed sit-down between China’s Xi Jinping, Trump and Putin may remain a mystery, but no meeting at the APEC conference will attract more attention.
While Putin has pushed for talks on Ukraine, Trump this week suggested the focus would be on denuclearisation and ending his faltering war in Iran.
Analysts who spoke to AFP cautioned expectations should be kept to a minimum.
“The symbolism... will account for a good portion of its substance,” the Brookings Institution’s Ryan Hass told AFP.
While he expects Xi and Putin to give Trump “a respectful hearing” on arms control, Hass said they will likely only “agree on broad principles without committing to any follow-on actions”.
Wang Wen, dean of Renmin University’s Chongyang Institute for Financial Studies, agreed major outcomes were unlikely, calling it “a high probability that talks could end without a breakthrough”.
Separately, a meeting Trump once hoped for with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un appears dead in the water, with Pyongyang rejecting repeated overtures.
Eyeing AI safeguards
Artificial intelligence will be a hot topic at Apec, after Xi and Trump agreed in September to set up a “communication channel” for AI incidents.

Trump has repeatedly dismissed fears that AI could pose a threat to humanity. But despite the countries’ fierce tech rivalry, calls for cooperation are growing due to shared concerns regarding bioweapons and infrastructure hacking.
Xi in September said Washington and Beijing have a responsibility to “develop and manage AI for good and ensure that the development of AI is always under human control”.
Apec talks could build on the pair’s previous communication channel agreement, Stephen Wu, founder of Carthage Capital, told AFP.
“Both sides need an outcome, and a hotline is diplomacy’s cheapest: free to announce, free to ignore,” he said.

Meanwhile, a spying scandal enveloping Nvidia boss Jensen Huang, who was once widely expected to accompany Trump to Apec, threatens to cast a pall on AI discussions. US officials have accused him of sleeping with a woman they claim was working for Beijing.
Asean’s murky waters
In Manila, the Philippines’ year in the Asean chair looks set to come and go without fulfilling one of its top objectives: signing a South China Sea Code of Conduct (COC) with China.

The ongoing dispute over the waterway has cast a shadow over the bloc’s events all year. Philippine and Chinese sailors clashed a day before the start of a July summit, and a diplomatic row erupted at an October defence meeting.
One South-east Asian diplomat involved in summit preparations told AFP he did not see any agreement being reached in Manila.
Tang, the former Asean Studies Centre chief, said the code may have outlived its usefulness.

“If a COC was signed 10 years ago, 15 years ago, it’s meaningful. The COC today, I think, has lost its purpose... because the effects on the ground have changed,” he said, noting the militarisation of islands by both China and Vietnam.
Tariff relief? Not likely

e163141dbe2b07ab: The FreeBSD project's status team has published FreeBSD's third status report of 2026, showing plenty of ambitious work underway and a community still undecided on how to treat code from AI coding assistants.
The FreeBSD Status Report Third Quarter 2026 is a substantial document, with 51 entries from five teams covering 16 projects, plus six other sections with more detailed reports.

There are updates on the progress of the Sylve project, which is an attempt to bring a smooth polished GUI for managing FreeBSD virtualization hosts – something akin to Proxmox for FreeBSD. We mentioned this when we looked at the new Daemonarchy project last month. Another covers the new AppJail effort – a containerized app distribution system for FreeBSD, including for GUI apps, which aims for something broadly comparable to Snap, Flatpak and AppImage on Linux.
In other words, interesting and quite radical stuff is happening in the FreeBSD space.

What this particular LLM-skeptical vulture was most interested to see, though, was an update on the internal discussion about how to handle code generated by AI coding assistants in the project. We first reported on this vexed subject back in September 2025 and no final answer has yet been published.

NetBSD banned AI-generated code in 2024 and although the bot-boosters say this will doom it to irrelevance, as we reported last month, the project is thriving. Also back in October, we looked at OpenBSD 8.0, whose launch materials are full of mockery for AI users.

Under the FreeBSD Core Team section, there is a subsection headed "FreeBSD Developer AI survey." The survey was created by Baptiste Daroussin, and received 140 responses. Although the percentages show that there is some resistance to AI, there are hints here as to why it’s taking so long. Some project committers are against it, yet many more are proponents. Since there are only seven bullet points, we thought we would quote them in full:

Policy: 88 percent want the Project to adopt a policy, either a formal, written policy (49 percent) or light guidance and best practices (39 percent). Six percent said that AI should be explicitly discouraged, and three percent that the existing contribution rules are sufficient.

AI-assisted code: 35 percent said it must be disclosed, 25 percent that it must be reviewed more strictly than human code, 22 percent that it should be treated like any other contribution, and 16 percent that it should be rejected outright.

Safeguards: mandatory human review (78 percent) and mandatory disclosure (69 percent) were requested most often, followed by provenance or licensing documentation (47 percent) and mandatory testing (39 percent).

Disclosure: 84 percent want AI use disclosed, either always (48 percent) or when its involvement is significant (36 percent). 79 percent want AI-assisted commits marked in the commit log, and 56 percent prefer a tag that names the tool.

Concerns: the main concerns about quality are correctness and subtle bugs (39 percent, licensing and provenance (26 percent), and maintainability (21 percent). 75 percent are somewhat or very concerned about copyright and licensing.

Principles: accountability, meaning that a human remains responsible (91 percent), and transparency (78 percent) were selected most often, and preserving code quality was the top-ranked goal for a policy.
Other uses: 65 percent would allow AI-generated documentation with human review. 54 percent would allow AI tools on Project infrastructure, most of them with restrictions, and 29 percent would not.

Only six percent for explicit discouragement, 16 percent for outright rejection, and 35 percent against LLM-generated documentation. This plus the usual sort of calls for responsible use and disclosure, concerns about copyright issues, and so on.

The Reg is strongly reminded of the Debian developer poll we reported on in August. This had no fewer than four slightly different AI-refusal options out of eight, and despite the Condorcet voting method it uses, the result was giving permission to use bots.

With such relatively weak opposition, we suspect that FreeBSD will go the same way as Debian: tell developers to be careful, but allow bot usage, resulting in LLM-extruded code being committed into the project. ®

555c0bc21f885b90: Encountered some odd SQL Server connection behavior since the October update? There might be a culprit… Microsoft has admitted that a change has caused linked server queries to fail to close connections.

Linked servers via OLE DB providers have been around for years and are a useful way of, for example, using additional data sources in queries. Once a provider is added, SQL Server can open a connection to grab data, and close it again when the query is complete. Or, at least, that's the theory.

The problem is that after the October 13 (KB5126646) update, connections created by SQL Server linked server queries might remain open. According to Microsoft, "As additional queries are performed, connections to external databases can accumulate instead of closing as expected.
"This can slow or degrade server performance after prolonged run time."
You think? Administrators will likely have already noted a suspicious number of open connections to external databases on affected systems.

Microsoft said the issue affects SQL Server linked server queries that use OLE DB providers to connect to external databases. It gave PostgreSQL and Oracle as examples of connections known to be affected.
And the fix? "If idle connections can be identified, it is possible to manually close them to temporarily relieve server load.
"It is also possible to temporarily restore system stability by restarting the SQL service."
The Windows behemoth went on to state the obvious: "However, these steps can also interrupt active queries or transactions, and the problem can resurface again after sufficient operation time."

Bouncing a SQL Server to deal with connection leakage is less than ideal, although it would at least be a good failover test and, let's face it, having to restart Microsoft services regularly is something many administrators will be all too familiar with.
There is a mitigation available, although only through Microsoft support for business. Otherwise, an out-of-band update should be along within the next few days to deal with the problem.
According to Microsoft, the technical glitch affects every version of Windows except Windows 11 26H2, stretching back to Windows 10 1809 and LTSC 2019, and Windows Server from 2025 back to 2012.

Microsoft, or rather the unfortunate souls responsible for administering their server products, has not had the best time of late. The October 2026 Windows Server update left some Exchange Servers wobbling until either a Registry edit was made or a fix was applied as part of the November update. ®

986fe7d205dc3b07: European tech buyers are increasingly choosing cybersecurity vendors from their own continent in a bid to reduce their reliance on American technology.
Digital sovereignty isn't only prompting enterprise customers to question their clouds of choice, it is also reshaping other parts of the industry too, and the shift is marked.

According to sales figures compiled by Context, distributor sales in EMEA of cybersecurity products from EU-headquartered vendors jumped 35 percent in the two years to calendar Q3 2026. Total cybersecurity sales grew up 10 percent over the same period, and sales by US-run companies went up just 8 percent.

That growth is from a relatively small base, though EU vendors gained nearly three percentage points to reach 15 percent of tracked sales by value. There is still a long way to go as US-headquartered vendors accounted for 62 percent.

The trend coincides with a loss of trust in the Trump administration among customers outside of America, after it cosied up to autocratic rulers while criticizing and punishing allies with tariffs and more.

Context stopped short of assigning blame. It said organizations are reviewing their reliance on third-party tech in light of EU compliance regimes: the NIS2 Directive and Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA).

NIS2, transposed into national law in October 2024, requires organizations in the bloc to raise their common level of security in the face of digital threats and risks to critical infrastructure. DORA, introduced in January last year, is designed to strengthen cyber security in the financial sector.

"Digital sovereignty is becoming a buying decision. As customers and resellers get clearer about what it means in practice, they're asking who holds the encryption keys, who can access sensitive logs and where that data is stored," said Context veep of research Joe Turner.

"We're seeing a measurable shift in the EMEA channel. EU vendors gained nearly three points of sales share in two years. An organization can keep its existing identity platform and still choose a European supplier to manage its security logs. That's the kind of decision that gives European vendors an opening."

The stats indicate that EU-HQd vendors comprised 92 percent of tracked sales in security awareness training, 82 percent in vulnerability management, and 52 percent for SIEM and log management. US-headquartered companies held into 74 percent of identity and access management sales and 54 percent of cloud security sales.

The Reg has asked Context for UK-specific figures to see whether British customers are also voting with their wallets for European alternatives. That certainly isn’t the case for tech purchases in the British public sector, despite Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s professed desire to buy British.
Data released yesterday by the Institute for Public Policy Research showed just £1 in every £6 spent by government with the biggest technology suppliers goes to Brit businesses.
Still, Burnham only came to power in July so there is time yet for him to put his money where his mouth is.

Sovereign AI is another area of concern for enterprise customers. Analyst Omdia said last month that despite the marketing adjective meaning "local assets," almost a third AI providers disclose no proof of sovereignty, and some "expect enterprise to pay for audits to verify their claims."

Omdia also found that 80 percent of contracts say network resilience is "out of providers control or responsibility," and "US-headquartered AI providers offer better service transparency and contract terms than a majority of local sovereign AI providers, with providers in India a notable exception."
Sovereign services in Omdia's classification include data residency, operational autonomy, jurisdictional sovereignty, and technological autonomy.

"Local hosting is not sovereignty. Serious providers must demonstrate their credibility through transparent operations, fair contracts and proof of competence. That includes the network, because data in transit must be sovereign too," said Camille Mendler, research director for telco B2B at Omdia.
Someone should tell Microsoft and Anthropic. ®

94cbf139538e3243: More than 1,600 Rockstar Games employees in the UK will begin voting on union recognition on Thursday, with the ballot kicking off just a week before the long-awaited launch of Grand Theft Auto VI.

The ballot, which opens on November 12 and runs until November 26, will determine whether Rockstar formally recognizes the Rockstar Game Workers Union, part of the Independent Workers Union of Great Britain (IWGB). Nearly all UK employees below director level are eligible to vote.
If successful, the union would become the largest recognized union in the UK games industry, giving workers a collective voice.

The proposed recognition agreement follows four months of negotiations between Rockstar management and employees. It would allow workers to negotiate over pay, overtime, pensions, bonuses, leave and other employment conditions, while securing consultation rights over HR policies and AI.

The vote comes at a particularly busy time for Rockstar, with GTA VI finally due to arrive on November 19, more than 13 years after its predecessor. The game is expected to be one of the biggest entertainment launches in history, although the people responsible for making it have rather more immediate concerns than sales records.

"I am incredibly proud of the work we've put into making this game. I'm also proud of the union we've built here. For me, those two things are connected," said Nestor Uriate, an animation programmer and Rockstar Game Workers Union representative.

"We care deeply about the games we make, and we want to make sure we can continue doing that work in an environment where we're respected, have a meaningful say over our conditions and can feel secure about our futures."

The vote follows a year of bad blood between Rockstar and the IWGB. The union accused the GTA developer of union busting after it fired 31 members in October 2025, claiming they had been singled out for taking part in a private Discord group.
Rockstar denied the allegations, insisting the workers were dismissed for gross misconduct rather than their union activities.

The dispute subsequently reached an employment tribunal, where Rockstar unsuccessfully attempted to have blacklisting allegations struck from the case. Closing submissions are expected on November 17 and 18, meaning the legal proceedings will reach their final stages just as GTA VI prepares to hit shelves.

Despite the ongoing dispute, Rockstar's head of publishing, Jennifer Kolbe, recently indicated that management would respect the outcome of the recognition vote, telling Bloomberg: "We go where the team goes. So if they want a union, they will have a union."
The union campaign has also attracted support from elsewhere in the games industry, including SAG-AFTRA and the Communications Workers of America (CWA), which represents workers at Blizzard.
Alex Marshall, president of the IWGB, said the vote was an opportunity for Rockstar employees to take greater control over their working conditions.

"What happens at Rockstar matters beyond the studio. Workers across the games industry are watching, and this ballot is an opportunity to show what can be achieved when people come together, organize and build the collective power to shape their own working lives."

For Rockstar, November was already shaping up to be a big month. By the time GTA VI has been in players' hands for a week, the company should also know whether its UK workforce has voted to secure a formal seat at the negotiating table. ®

37248e32a1da39b1: A new extension brings a working global menu bar to the GNOME desktop, even for some apps that don’t have menu bars at all.

Orbit Global Menu is a new GNOME extension that gives the GNOME desktop a feature it was intentionally designed without, and one that some users miss very badly – this vulture being one of them. It adds a working global menu bar to the GNOME top panel. We suspect this is something that will cause strongly contrasting opinions among many GNOME users: some will by puzzled why anyone would bother, while others may think "at last!" and rush to try it.

There have been other attempts to do this before, and the Reg FOSS desk has tried several of them, but we never found one that worked with the majority of applications. Our fondness for this UI feature was visible in the two-part series we wrote in September on how to customize Xfce and then in part two how to get the global menu working with more apps.

The problem is getting worse over time, as in recent versions (since GNOME 40 and Gtk4), the GNOME human-interface guidelines encourage smartphone-style hamburger menus, replacing the traditional horizontal menu bar. It is tricky to add global menu bar support to apps that lack a menu bar, but Orbit's developer "Unmade" found a rather labor-intensive solution. The menu bar applet contains maps of keyboard controls for 292 different apps, so it can show a menu all on its own and then send those apps simulated keystrokes to operate it. It's not the programs' full menu trees, just a subset of them, but it works.

It's also not the most elegant solution, but it is a solution and it works. We tried it on Ubuntu 26.10 and every app in the full install worked to at least some extent. If you are willing and able to build and install a small additional connector, it lets the global-menu applet talk to lots more applications.

The GNOME shell is unusual among open source desktop environments, to an extent that we have criticized before. GNOME Shell was designed with a distinctive look and feel of its own, unlike almost all other desktops. It has a minimalist, stripped-down layout that doesn't look or work quite like anything else, and it's intentionally not very customizable. To change how GNOME works means writing new Javascript code, then packaging it as an extension that users can install from the GNOME Extensions website. This requires both a browser extension and a "native host messaging" connector to be installed into the underlying OS – or a purpose-written app. By default, the desktop comes with neither.

The end result is that GNOME lends a visual identity to the Linux desktop, one that is clear and distinct from either Windows or macOS. (Back in 2013, this vulture argued that when Microsoft threatened to sue multiple Linux vendors over infringing Windows UI patents, some 20 years ago, this UI fragmentation was just what the company wanted.) GNOME 2 was the Linux world's default desktop. GNOME Shell was controversial in its early days, and lost pole position, but it has since won it back. Today, GNOME is the default desktop on all the major distros: Ubuntu, Fedora and Red Hat Enterprise Linux and the RHELatives, as well as Debian and SUSE, all default to GNOME.

GNOME does away with a lot of features that are significant functional parts of other graphical desktops. For instance, it has no desktop icons, no system tray or defined place for status indicators, and neither GNOME nor GNOME-compliant applications have menu bars, either inside windows (Microsoft style) or in the top panel (Apple macOS style). This is disorienting and confusing for those used to controlling software mainly using their menus – but now, that's mainly older hands. This design suits those who grew up on smartphones and tablets, or who feel more comfortable with their stripped-back keyboardless UI than a full desktop WIMP, which can be overwhelming to newbies and non-techies.

If you've followed the evolution of graphical desktops for some 40 years, as this gray-plumed vulture has, some trends are very apparent that aren't so clear if you came in once evolution was underway.

Apple introduced the first global menu bar in the Lisa, and improved on that in the Macintosh. DR GEM copied it very early on, but Apple sued and DR changed the PC version of GEM to be less Mac-like. Microsoft's Windows came along after this, and moved menu bars inside windows instead. When Apple acquired NeXT in 1996, it moved NeXTstep's patent-avoidant vertical menus back to a global bar at the top, along with the clock and some status indicators. There they remain, 30 years later. In 2007, it launched the iPhone, containing a very cut-down OS based on OS X, replacing the Finder with a cut-down version of the Dashboard layer from OS X 10.4. The panel remained, shorn of its menus, which were too fiddly for a small screen.

As The Register mentioned in 2017, in its preliminary releases, Android started out as a keypad-driven Java phone that looked and worked very much like BlackBerry. When the iPhone appeared, Google changed course. The new Android UI resembled iOS, complete with that top panel, still without menus. GNOME 3.0 was not far behind: in 2009 the team promised a revamp of the user experience, and in 2011, launched GNOME 3.0. It too has the fixed top panel — now huge on a laptop or desktop landscape screen – and mostly empty.

Now that top panel regains its original 1983 function. We're rather impressed by the Orbit global menu. It does the job, and it even works with apps that don't have menu bars. It's not perfect: for instance, over-long menus have to scroll, and may fail to do so if new submenus appear.

The GitHub repository has extensive instructions, including how to build and install the optional connector module that lets more apps export their real menus to the extension. It also tells you how to instruct some apps, notably Firefox, that there is a global menu for it to use. We are saddened to note that, as is so often the case, Wayland gets in the way here.

It works rather well with some other extensions, too. With a menu bar, GNOME's strangely centered clock seems out of place, but several extensions, such as Frippery Move Clock, shove it over to the right where we still feel it belongs. If you prefer a lighter-colored panel and dock, it also plays nicely with Blur my Shell. ®
1bc4406ceb8eb745: GEORGE TOWN, Nov 12 — A majority of PBA Holdings Bhd’s shareholders have approved Penang Water Supply Corporation’s (PBAPP) proposal to purchase a minimum of 300 million litres per day (MLD) of treated water from Perak starting in 2032.

PBA Holdings and PBAPP chairman Chow Kon Yeow said PBA has obtained the approval needed to fulfil a condition precedent in the Bulk Water Supply Agreement (BWSA) between PBAPP and Prasarana Air dan Irigasi Perak Sdn Bhd (PAIP).

“At this general meeting, the board of directors’ proposal was approved by a majority vote, with 97.93 per cent voting in favour of PBAPP’s proposed purchase of treated water under the Penang-Perak Water Supply Scheme, as we have announced many times,” he said at a press conference after an extraordinary general meeting attended by shareholders today.
He said that after obtaining the approval, PBA will inform Bursa Malaysia and PAIP so that steps can be taken to commence the project.

“Under the agreement, we have a date for receiving the treated water — March 31, 2032. That is the date by which the project must be completed and treated water delivered to Penang, or to PBAPP, up to the Perak-Penang border and beyond that point, it is PBA’s responsibility to distribute the treated water we receive from Perak,” he said.
Chow, who is also Penang chief minister, said a group, representing minority shareholders, had submitted a letter in advance raising issues that was addressed during the meeting.
“Apart from the minority shareholder group, the other shareholders present did not raise any additional questions beyond those raised by the group,” he said.
As for the setting of water tariffs, Chow said this was already specified in the BWSA and that PAIP must fulfil one of the pre-conditions in obtaining approval from SPAN for the proposed tariff.

“That could also cause the project to fail. If Perak does not obtain SPAN’s approval for the proposed tariff, and for the capacity charge and other charges to be collected through the water tariff, the agreement will not proceed,” he said.
He said Perak has until 2035 to obtain SPAN’s approval for the tariff.

”If they cannot do so, we can say that we are walking away because SPAN has not approved it. They would then have to go back to SPAN and propose a new tariff until SPAN accepts the proposal,” he said.
He said this is a condition precedent of the agreement that Perak has to fulfil before the project can proceed.

861e01e051d3cad7: FRANKFURT, Nov 12 — German engineering giant Siemens posted record annual profit on Thursday and said it saw growth ahead as the artificial intelligence boom sweeps up European companies in its supply chain.

US tech giants such as Microsoft and Meta have together invested hundreds of billions of dollars in AI data centres, boosting the fortunes of companies like Siemens that make much of the electrical and cooling equipment needed to operate the sites.

Swiss competitor ABB in October posted order growth of 40 per cent for the three months to end-September, while France’s Schneider Electric in the same month said sales growth over the period had beaten expectations.

Reporting results for its fiscal year to end-September, Siemens said its core industrial profit, which strips out some effects such as last year’s sale of motor-maker Innomotics, rose 13 per cent to €13.3 billion (RM60.1 billion), or US$14.7 billion for the year.

Siemens said it expected further growth in the current business year, guiding for sales growth of between nine and 11 per cent across the company as well as broadly stable or higher profit margins at its two biggest divisions.

In the longer term, Siemens said it was now targeting sales growth of between seven and 11 per cent a year, up from six to nine, as well as annual earnings per share growth of at least 10 per cent, up from single-digit growth.
“Fiscal 2026 was an outstanding year for Siemens,” CEO Roland Busch said in a statement.
“We are providing an ambitious outlook for fiscal 2027 and are raising our group-level mid-term targets.”

For the fourth quarter, orders – an indicator of future sales – at Siemens’ smart infrastructure business rose 40 per cent to €8.67 billion (RM39.2 billion), helped by “numerous larger contract wins from data centre customers”, Siemens said.
Orders at Siemens’ digital industries division, which makes software for engineering and automation, rose 16 per cent over the same period to €6.41 billion (RM29 billion).
Under Busch, Siemens has pivoted towards higher-margin software products in recent years as part of its “Industrial AI” strategy. — AFP

5593d2aaccddb93f: LONDON, Nov 12 — Britain’s economy expanded in line with expectations in the third quarter, official data showed Thursday, as spending on the AI boom helped offset the fallout from the US-Iran war.
Gross domestic product grew 0.7 per cent in the July-September period, up from a revised expansion of 0.5 per cent in the second quarter, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said in a statement.

ff47cee33ad05fda: TAIPEI, Nov 12 — Taiwanese tech giant Foxconn on Thursday reported a record net profit for the third quarter, as the global buildout of data centres fuels demand for the AI servers needed to operate them.
The world’s largest electronics contract manufacturer has gone beyond making low-margin iPhones to producing AI servers for US tech titan Nvidia, as well as electric vehicles and robots.
Its shares and those of other tech firms plunged last week after the Democrats’ sweep of Congress in the US midterms would allow them to ramp up AI regulation and slow the data centre expansion.

Foxconn partner Nvidia has also weighed on sentiment, with US media reporting the company’s board is preparing to oust CEO Jensen Huang after revelations of his extramarital affairs, including with an alleged Chinese spy.
Foxconn said net profit for July-September hit NT$77.5 billion (RM9.8 billion), or US$2.4 billion (RM9.8 billion), up 34 per cent on-year.
The result beat estimates of NT$70.3 billion (RM8.9 billion) in a Bloomberg survey of analysts.
Revenue for the three months was up 39 per cent at NT$7.7 trillion (RM970 billion).
Chief Financial Officer David Huang said Foxconn’s “third-quarter revenue, operating income, net income, and earnings per share all reached record quarterly highs”.
“AI servers have become Foxconn’s most important growth driver,” Chairman Young Liu told a briefing.
Looking ahead, he said “we remain very confident in next year’s operations and believe growth will continue”.
But he warned of stubborn bottlenecks in the AI and consumer electronics supply chains, with overall demand “still expected to outpace supply heading into next year”.
That will mean “tight supply-demand conditions may persist for some time”, he said.
Foxconn has a longstanding partnership with Nvidia.
In one of their collaborations, the companies are working to build an “AI factory supercomputer” in Taiwan.
Governments and tech giants have been pouring huge sums into building data centres that can train and run AI tools such as chatbots, image generators and agents that can execute tasks.
The buildout has turbocharged business for Foxconn – which makes the servers used in the centres – but any slowdown could potentially hurt the company’s bottom line.
Data centres require large amounts of electricity, placing increased pressure on grids often still reliant on fossil fuels.
In many cases, they also ramp up strain on water resources used to cool computing equipment.
A backlash is growing worldwide against their environmental impacts, and there are also concerns over noise, pollution, their appearance and how many jobs the facilities actually create. — AFP
b5a7a069ea875674: There is a long list of people who have been, or still are, under detention in their own homes around the world.
Many are former heads of state or government. Apart from Najib Razak, we can count Myanmar’s Aung San Suu Kyi and former French president Nicolas Sarkozy among them.
Like Najib, Sarkozy was convicted of a criminal offence. On the other hand, Suu Kyi is being detained for her opposition to the military dictatorship that continues to hold sway in Myanmar.
Another politician who also lived at home but as a prisoner was ex-Argentine president Cristina Fernández de Kirchner.
Unlike Malaysia, both Argentina and France already had provisions in their legal systems for home detention when their respective leaders — in this instance de Kirchner and Sarkozy — were sentenced.

In Argentina, the provision for house arrest goes back a long way — all the way back to 1886 when its first National Criminal Code was put in place. There have been several updates — in 1921, 1996 and subsequently in 2008.
According to Argentina.gob.ar, the official portal of the Argentine State, several conditions must be met before a prisoner qualifies for home detention.
He or she must be suffering from a terminal illness, or a malady that “cannot be adequately treated in prison” but does not require hospitalisation.
A person with a disability, making him vulnerable to inhumane or degrading treatment in a prison environment or any person aged over 70 also qualifies. So do pregnant women and caregiving mothers.
At age 72, de Kirchner qualifies on age alone.
In France, house arrest is provided for under Article 142-5 of the French Code of Criminal Procedure.

It states that a person convicted of a criminal offence and sentenced to a year or less in jail can be confined to his home under strict conditions. The prisoner must also show that he does not pose a flight risk.
Sarkozy was sentenced to three years but qualified anyway because two of those three years were suspended.
As far as we know, Najib is neither ill nor pregnant. He does not have any young child to watch over either.
At age 76, former Negeri Sembilan menteri besar Isa Samad is still serving out his six-year prison sentence for corruption. Najib is three years younger than him.
Even if we pick a leaf or two from the Argentine and French playbooks on home detention, Najib does not qualify on any front.

In September, Najib was granted a conditional pardon by the Yang di-Pertuan Agong under which he could serve out the remainder of his six-year sentence in the SRC International case under house arrest.
The condition was that he paid the RM50 million fine. Umno managed to raise the sum and the fine was paid on Nov 6.
Najib is already home to continue serving his sentence, but it is not too late to start thinking about putting in place provisions for house arrest.
Chances are there will be more to come.

05a995930b01ced5: HONG KONG, Nov 12 — Asian stocks fell Thursday as investors kept a nervous eye on Nvidia whose influential boss Jensen Huang faces a probe into an affair with a woman accused of spying for China.

Companies linked to the artificial intelligence sector have enjoyed a healthy bounce in recent days after last week’s selloff sparked by regulatory concerns following the Democratic sweep of Congress.

The upcoming IPO of Anthropic and positive earnings from the likes of ChatGPT-maker OpenAI and data centre operator CoreWeave – which soothed worries about its financial health – have reinforced optimism.
Chipmakers SK hynix, Samsung, Kioxia and TSMC have led the surge in Asia, even amid rising expectations for a series of US interest rate hikes.

Tokyo, Seoul, Hong Kong, Shanghai, Taipei, Sydney, Singapore, Mumbai, Bangkok and Manila all dropped, though there were gains in Jakarta and Wellington.

Traders’ nerves are being tested by the crisis at Nvidia, with co-founder and CEO Huang facing the boot after he admitted a relationship with Alice Huang, a senior executive at Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed.
US intelligence reportedly circulated a memo in spring alleging Alice Huang was an asset of China’s Ministry of State Security.
The New York Times reported Wednesday that Huang was also involved in a second extramarital affair, with the company’s vice president of health care, Kimberly Powell.
The tech company’s board was preparing to meet as soon as Wednesday to determine Huang’s future, according to the Wall Street Journal, which quoted people familiar with the matter.

Huang has built Nvidia to be one of the world’s biggest and most important companies, designing advanced chips crucial to the AI buildout that has helped drive stock markets to record highs and boosted economies around the world.
Succession concerns
“Nvidia has spent years convincing investors that it is one of the most important companies in the AI revolution,” wrote Charu Chanana at Saxo Markets.
“Now, the biggest question surrounding the company is not about its chips, competitors or earnings.
“It is about its founder.”
She said Huang was key to the firm’s future, including dealings with governments.
“Nvidia’s technological advantage would not disappear with his departure,” she added.
“Its CUDA software ecosystem, product capabilities and customer relationships remain formidable strengths.
“But an abrupt exit without a credible succession plan could force investors to reassess how much of Nvidia’s future depends on Huang personally.”
Nvidia’s shares slid more than eight per cent in after-hours US trade, and are down around 20 per cent since news of the affair broke at the end of last month.
Oil prices inched down as investors kept tabs on the Middle East crisis, with hopes still high that the US and Iran can reach a deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

4dcaee04b6caac45: The school gardens are helping alleviate food insecurity while providing learning opportunities and empowering community members
Originally published on Global Voices
Students of Blessed Bilingual Education Centre preparing the farm. Photo by Support Humanity Cameroon. Used with permission.

Students of Blessed Bilingual Education Centre in Ebang, Cameroon’s Centre Region, have recorded their first harvest of the 2026–2027 school year. Through the Climate Change and Innovation Club, an initiative introduced in 2024 by Support Humanity Cameroon (SUHUCAM) to connect environmental education with practical action, students planted huckleberry in their school garden at the start of the academic year in September. Like them, pupils in Cameroon’s North West Region are managing school gardens and growing food using regenerative practices such as minimal tillage, composting, organic manure and fruit-tree grafting.

Cameroon continues to face a decade-long humanitarian crisis, contributing to food insecurity in the Anglophone regions and Far North, while displacing thousands of families. Earlier this year, the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies reported worsening hunger among nearly 6,000 Cameroonian households following an assessment. More than 3.3 million people were struggling to find enough food, while about 64 percent of households experienced severe food insecurity.

Children are among those affected. Nationwide, 29 percent of children under five experience chronic malnutrition. Beyond its nutritional consequences, food insecurity can also affect children’s ability to learn and participate in school activities.

According to the Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO), hunger can impair concentration and memory and affect classroom attendance. In February 2026, the organisation reported that only 2.8 percent of primary school pupils in Cameroon received a free hot meal at school, highlighting the limited reach of school lunch programmes.
Conflict, climate-related disasters, agricultural losses and rising staple food prices are among the main drivers of this crisis.
School gardens in action
To combat persistent food insecurity, educators and nonprofit organisations are partnering to teach children how to grow their own food.

In Bamenda, North West region of Cameroon, the Youth Association for Climate Action (YACA) runs the ADAPT Programme, which engages 70 pupils from two nursery and primary schools. Created after a survey revealed that few schools had gardens or provided environmental education, the ADAPT Club has established gardens with five sections: nurseries, vegetables, fruit trees, composting and tubers.

Muluh Kelly Vughose, Programme coordinator for ADAPT, says pupils are involved in more than just planting. “Our volunteers, together with the teachers and pupils, designed each garden. Children are also involved in learning basic agricultural skills like plantain propagation and grafting of fruit trees.” The club holds two sessions each week, lasting about two hours.

In the same region, in Nkambe and neighbouring villages, pupils from six primary and two secondary schools are learning agricultural skills through the Smart School Gardens Project, launched by Youth Development Organisation – Yodo Cameroon. Schools have received wheelbarrows, watering cans and compost manure to support the project.

“During the two years of implementation, I have watched these pupils and students care for plants from seed germination until harvest,” says Ekoaba Cevie, Yodo Cameroon’s Programme Coordinator. The gardens produce cabbage, huckleberry, carrots and Irish potatoes.

Meanwhile, SUHUCAM’s regenerative school garden programme in the Centre region combines fruit trees, including guava, soursop, orange and papaya, with plantains and produce such as huckleberry, cabbage and waterleaf. Through these activities, pupils are learning techniques such as composting, plant propagation and grafting.

Children are embracing the school gardens with enthusiasm, discovering the importance of food production and sustainability through practical experience. Queeninver Ngwangung, SUHUCAM’s Youth and Advocacy Lead, explains:

“Rather than simply teaching students about sustainable agriculture, food security or climate action, we give them opportunities to practice these concepts,” she said. “Through growing food, managing organic waste and caring for their gardens, we have observed that students have learnt that environmental solutions can begin with everyday actions within their own schools.”

For Amang Mael, a Form Three student, seeing vegetables grow on an abandoned plot behind his school has been particularly exciting. “Since we planted the vegetables, I have been so eager to harvest. We add organic manure to all our crops so they can be healthy.”

Another student, Kouba Princesse, believes the garden can contribute to the fight against hunger. “Now that I know how to grow my own vegetables, I will not have to depend on buying from the market all the time,” she says. Some kids have taken the practice home, where they maintain small gardens and use plastic bottles for drip irrigation during the dry season. Other students also say the experience has sparked an interest in pursuing careers in agriculture.
Supporting community nutrition

In 2025, the ADAPT Club produced approximately 45 kilogrammes of dry compost from biodegradable waste. At the end of each planting cycle, YACA organises a Mini School Garden Market Day, where parents and community members can buy the harvest. “Income gained is reinvested in the next planting cycle,” says Muluh Kelly.

At SUHUCAM, the harvests serve nutritional and educational purposes. Students eat fruits from the gardens, while vegetables are sold to purchase seeds and fund their continued management. Some students take extra produce home to establish household gardens.
After two years with two regenerative school garden cycles, SUHUCAM’s Climate Change and Innovation Club has benefitted thousands of households and planted over 400 trees.

In Nkambe, pupils involved in Yodo Cameroon’s project also sell their harvests to community members at affordable prices. The proceeds have helped schools purchase basic educational materials, including chalk and exercise books. Ekoaba Cevie, Yodo Cameroon’s project manager says:

The gardens have become practical outdoor classrooms. Not only are the children learning new agricultural skills, but they are also gaining an appreciation for nature, responsible environmental practices and sustainable resource management.

The nutritional potential of school-based production is also evident in other initiatives. In 2025, an integrated school production programme supported by FAO in Cameroon’s East and South regions established 18 school gardens. The programme produced 236,859 kilogrammes of vegetables, alongside eggs and fish, helping provide weekly healthy meals to 10,833 students. Children, teachers and community members also received training in sustainable agriculture, hygiene and nutrition.

Nkimih Clinton, a researcher at the Institute of Agricultural Research for Development (IRAD), says regenerative practices, such as those deployed in the community gardens, can improve soil health and support sustainable agriculture. Composting, mulching, crop rotation and organic manure, he explains, “can contribute to maintaining the health of pieces of land” for crop production. However, he cautions against expecting small-scale school gardens to eliminate hunger entirely.

Although they may not provide all the food pupils need, they can improve dietary quality by supplying vegetables, legumes and fruits rich in essential vitamins and minerals. “School gardens can be used as a source of production of micro-nutrients to complement basic staples (cassava, maize, rice) provided by parents,” Clinton says.
Challenges to overcome

Despite their benefits, maintaining school gardens remains difficult. Programme coordinators say unpredictable rainfall makes it harder to plan planting activities and sustain crop production. Changing weather conditions can also contribute to pest outbreaks and seed shortages.

Maintaining the gardens during school holidays is another challenge, as pupils are less available to care for the crops. These difficulties can interrupt children’s opportunities to follow the entire production cycle, from planting to harvesting. Expanding the initiatives will therefore require coordinated support from government officials, agricultural research institutions and development partners.
Schools need funding, reliable water supply, farming tools, quality seeds and technical assistance to maintain productive gardens throughout the year.
Government and policy support

Cameroon has previously taken steps to promote environmental education in schools. In 2018, the Ministry of Secondary Education and the Israeli Ambassador to Cameroon launched a Green School campaign that planted 300 trees in 30 schools.

In May 2023, the country launched the second phase of the Classes Vertes project, a three-year initiative developed by FAO in partnership with the Special Council Support Fund for Mutual Assistance (FEICOM) and several government ministries. Targeting 80 schools across the Far North, North, Adamawa, East and South regions, the programme sought to promote vegetable production, fish farming and poultry farming to improve children’s access to nutritious food. It also included tree planting and initiatives to build school canteens, water, sanitation, and hygiene facilities, with an allocated budget of approximately FCFA 722 million (USD 1.2 million).

The government’s commitment to improving children’s access to nutritious food is also reflected in its National School Feeding Strategy for 2025–2030, which aims to expand school meals and strengthen links between schools and local food producers.

Officials hope the program will reach one million learners by 2030. In July 2026, the government, through the Ministry of Basic Education, signed a EUR 3.6 million (USD 4 million) agreement with the World Food Programme (WFP) to expand home-grown school feeding in the Adamawa, East and Far North regions. The 2026–2029 programme is expected to provide nutritious meals to nearly 11,000 children in ten public primary schools while creating market opportunities for 600 smallholder farmers.

Meanwhile, experts believe school gardens can be replicated across Cameroon but stress that their implementation must reflect the country’s different agro-ecological zones. Rather than adopting a uniform approach, schools need solutions suited to their agro-ecological zones.

While school gardens may not independently resolve Cameroon’s food insecurity challenges, they offer opportunities to strengthen children’s nutritional knowledge, promote sustainable agriculture and encourage household food production. Their long-term impact, however, will depend on sustained investment, technical support and policies that enable more schools to establish and maintain these initiatives.

a865d7bae4f04a4d: Accurate, up-to-date climate projections are essential for planning decisions that enhance the resilience of power grids, protect public health, maximize agricultural yields, and more. Now, MIT researchers have developed a technique that streamlines the production of fast, trustworthy, and adaptable artificial intelligence models for climate prediction. These specialized AI models, known as climate emulators, can rapidly simulate the effects of human activities onto a future climate, predicting impacts on temperatures or sea level, for example.  Because emulators run in a matter of seconds, scientists use them to efficiently test thousands of varied climate scenarios. This provides more reliable estimates and can identify unexpected outcomes of regional interventions. The MIT researchers developed a training technique that boosts the performance and adaptability of a climate emulator while using only a fraction of the data typically required. This significantly cuts production time for these practical scientific tools. They show that an emulator trained with a much smaller amount of carefully selected synthetic data accurately predicts outcomes of scenarios it did not see during training, while traditional emulators failed to adapt to new situations. “Climate emulators are especially well-suited for modeling policy-relevant scenarios. By using our method to generate optimized training data for an emulator, we can speed up the production of much more reliable emulators, so we can better trust their outputs for making policy decisions,” says Christoher Womack PhD ’26, who is now a postdoc at ETH Zurich and lead author of a paper on this technique. He is joined on the paper by Shahine Bouabid, a postdoc in the MIT Department of Earth, Atmospheric and Planetary Sciences (EAPS); Andrei Sokolov, a research scientist in MIT’s Center for Sustainability Science and Strategy (CS3); Popat Salunke, a postdoc in CS3; Glenn Flierl, a professor of oceanography in EAPS; Sebastian D. Eastham, an associate professor at Imperial College London; and senior author Noelle E. Selin, a professor in the MIT Institute for Data, Systems, and Society (IDSS) and EAPS, and director of CS3. The research appears this week in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.  Speedier surrogates Climate scientists typically use earth system models (ESMs) to make long-term projections about how global temperature or precipitation could change in response to varying greenhouse gas emissions. These enormous, physics-based models capture the major components and interactions of the earth’s climate in extreme detail. While powerful, ESMs can take months to run on a cluster of supercomputers — and that’s only to project one possible future climate scenario.  Selin and her collaborators design climate emulators, which are fast AI surrogate models that mimic the behavior of full-scale ESMs. Emulators help scientists test many scenarios, make more accurate forecasts, and explore specific pollutants and regional effects. “Climate emulators can run in just a few seconds, so it really expands what we can do in terms of exploring these future climate scenarios,” Womack says. When scientists design a climate emulator, they often train the AI model using a set of six to eight future scenarios based on realistic future trajectories of emissions. They must run each scenario through a full-scale ESM, making these datasets costly and time-consuming to generate.  The MIT researchers recently found that using realistic future scenarios as training data can lead to underperforming emulators that fail to predict unfamiliar or novel scenarios.  In this work, they developed an algorithm that generates a synthetic dataset of optimized climate scenarios tailored to boost one emulator’s predictive performance. “Our algorithm might generate some weird scenarios which look nothing like a realistic future, but we don’t care so much if the training scenarios are realistic. We are just trying to make the best possible dataset to train an emulator,” Womack says. Importantly, rather than needing to run a full ESM six or eight times to generate training data, a user would only need to run that model once. Tuning the training data  The researchers begin by generating an arbitrary climate scenario using a fast and simple climate model. They test how well their emulator can reproduce the results of that ESM, which gives them a measure of error. Because of the programming technique they used to build the training pipeline, they can iteratively update the training data to increase the emulator’s predictive skill. For instance, the algorithm could increase CO2 emissions dramatically in the year 2050 or rapidly decrease methane emissions in 2037. Then the optimization updates the training data until the emulator’s error level reaches a certain threshold. In the end, rather than resembling realistic scenarios in which emissions follow smooth trajectories, the synthetic data contain rapid variations. “By introducing these high-frequency wiggles and oscillations, our data enable the emulator to extract a lot more information about the overall system,” Womack explains. Their training algorithm outputs these emissions scenarios, which they can use to train an emulator that is more accurate and adaptable. “In the future, we are definitely going to see climates and scenarios we haven’t seen before. If we can simulate these different scenarios more robustly, we can provide more reliable information to the stakeholders who need it,” Selin says. For instance, an emulator trained with their technique can capture the effects of local pollutant control policies that reduce one pollutant while other emissions continue rising. The traditional emulators they evaluated failed this test.   In the long run, Womack hopes this work improves the usefulness of fast and adaptable climate emulators for policy formulation.  “This is such an important piece of the pipeline when it comes to creating useful tools that speak to stakeholder needs. Because the process of training an emulator can takes months or even years, the emulators we have are usually out-of-date. By cutting down that production time, I think this technique will be a game-changer in terms of getting updated tools into the hands of researchers and practitioners,” Selin adds. In the future, the researchers want to test their technique using an emissions scenario generated by a full ESM. They also want to apply it to other types of climate models and explore its effectiveness in broader machine learning and computer vision applications. This research was part of the Bringing Computation to the Climate Challenge (BC3) project and supported by Schmidt Sciences through the MIT Grand Challenges.
2df10f7c83c57d1f: Thousands of delegates, scientists and world leaders are gathered in Turkey for the latest United Nations climate summit, COP31. Their task is familiar: agree on how to cut greenhouse gas emissions and help countries cope with a warming planet. But after more than three decades of negotiations, global emissions remain stubbornly high and the world is on course to overshoot the critical threshold of 1.5°C of warming. So have these annual summits actually achieved anything? Dr Wesley Morgan, a climate diplomacy expert at UNSW Sydney, tells The Conversation Weekly podcast the answer is yes: The Paris Agreement is a monumental diplomatic achievement. Agreed in 2015, the treaty brought more than 190 countries together around shared climate goals. Morgan says it has helped shift the trajectory of global warming: We were headed towards utter catastrophe. We’re still headed towards some very dire circumstances and more ambition is needed, but it is better than it would have been without this global agreement. This year’s summit presents a particular diplomatic challenge for Australia because its climate and energy minister, Chris Bowen, is leading the negotiations. Morgan says Australia can “tell a very positive story about what’s happening domestically in Australia”, including by pointing to significant strides in rooftop solar, which is now installed on one in three homes. But Australia’s role as President of Negotiations at COP31 is controversial because Australia remains one of the world’s biggest exporters of coal and gas. “It really is a tightrope,” Morgan says. In September, the federal government approved an expansion of BHP’s Saraji coal mine in Queensland, while authorities in New South Wales gave the green light for a major Hunter Valley coal mine to keep operating until 2045. The negotiations also face a major setback following the Trump administration’s withdrawal in January from international climate cooperation. Yet Morgan notes that no other country has followed the United States out of the talks. Pressure from Europe and the Pacific European countries are expected to push for stronger commitments and stronger ambition from the COP 31 negotiations, following a summer of severe heatwaves and wildfires across the continent. “I think across Europe and in the UK, there’s a realisation that this is a clear and present danger now,” says Morgan. He also points to the influence of Pacific island nations as evidence that smaller countries can shape global agreements. In 2015, The Republic of the Marshall Islands helped build the High Ambition Coalition, which was instrumental in securing the Paris Agreement and its 1.5°C goal. For Pacific countries, Morgan says, that target is a matter of survival: The rallying cry from the Pacific is 1.5 to stay alive. One possible outcome from COP31 is a new global electrification target dubbed “35 by 35”: meeting 35% of the world’s final energy demand with electricity by 2035. Morgan sees it as another step towards economies powered by clean energy – and despite the setbacks, he insists the transition is already underway: There’s plenty of reasons for hope as well as reasons for despair. Disclosure statement Wesley Morgan is a fellow at the Climate Council of Australia. 01fe3273792f42dd: Ada satu pesona di rak buku ibu yang memikat dan menawan saya iaitu karya Raja Ali Haji, dengan judul Gurindam Dua Belas yang dipercayai dikarang atau tersebar sekitar tahun 1847.

Apa yang menyebabkan saya suka dengan gurindam adalah kerana ia tiada tentu bentuknya. Ia boleh jadi terikat atau tidak. Untuk gurindam dengan bentuk yang terikat, ia terdiri dari dua baris serangkap, mengandungi tiga hingga enam perkataan sebaris dengan rima a-a. Beberapa rangkap berkait akan menjadikan ia satu gagasan atau idea yang boleh dicerna. Sudah tentu Gurindam Dua Belas tersebut memukau saya.

Apabila saya menuliskan novel saya dengan tajuk Koro; salah satu pengikat atau pesona kepada karya ini dibina menerusi gurindam. Koro yang diterbitkan di Indonesia oleh Penerbit Circa pada tahun 2022, dan kemudian diterjemahkan ke bahasa Inggeris oleh Brigitte Bresson, dan diterbitkan oleh Penguin Random House sebagai The Koro Riots (2023) mengisahkan sebuah negara fiksional Republik Hujung Manani yang dilanda penyakit koro iaitu kaum lelakinya mengalami pengecutan alat kelamin mendadak. Sebagai sebuah satira politik, saya cuba mengungkapkan punca korupsi dan kemerosotan moral warga di republik itu dan bagaimana usaha-usaha protagonisnya Negarawan Sejati menegakkan keadilan dan melaksanakan reformasi.

Untuk meyakinkan khalayak akan kewujudan sebuah negara imaginasi ini saya menciptakan lagu kebangsaan, sejarahnya yang pernah ditakluk Perancis, memerikan sosiopolitik dan ekonomi, garis sempadan, dan paling penting negara ini juga memiliki warisan budaya sendiri iaitu gurindam.

Di republik fiksi ini, Gurindam Enam dikenali dan dihafal oleh rakyatnya. Gurindam Enam memerihalkan enam pasal yang mesti diambil kira oleh sesebuah negara untuk kekal merdeka, selamat hala tujunya dan terpelihara dari serangan musuh.

Sudah tentu saya sendiri tidak dapat menjelaskan bagaimanakah ilham atau idea Gurindam Enam ini datang mengalir, melainkan ia terbangun daripada bacaan lampau, perenungan yang bertahun-tahun dahulu disentak oleh karya-karya tradisional yang unggul. Dalam erti kata lain, minda saya secara separuh sedar ketika mengarang Koro dalam tahun 2000 ke 2022 itu melilau dan menerawang di galaksi atau cakerawala fikir yang luas. Ia menjelajah jauh tetapi akhirnya, kembali mendarat di rak buku ibu saya.
Gurindam Enam itu berbunyi begini:
"Dengarkan umat suatu rencana Mengarang kita gundah gulana
Barang gurindam kalau tak kena Sebabnya kita risau kan bangsa
Ini hikmah untuk pemerintah Petua dan syarat memberi faedah
Empat musuh sangat bedebah Ke atas rakyat berbuat payah
Gurindam Pasal Pertama Ada pun negeri hendak selamat Jangan dibiar panjat penjahat

Ada pun perangat ibaratkan kera Menekan rakyat menjarah harta

Barang dinasihat bijak pandai Kalau raja boleh dicanai

Apabila perangai teramat gopoh Menganga meminta perutnya penuh
Apabila ulama menjadi ular Maruah umat guris tercalar
Adapun jika agama terjual Lucutkan serban pukulkan capal
Gurindam Pasal Keempat Khabar diingat perangai Melayu Bangsa beringat menolak candu
Khabar candu macam aneka Ada ketagih hisapkan ganja
Khabar candu bermacam candu Ada ketagih perangai tak malu
Khabar perangai seamat keras Habis pantang semua diganas
Khabar ganas kepada orang Disangka Melayu umat terbilang
Khabar mana umat cemerlang Melayu ganas memijak orang
Khabar yang ganas usah diulang Perangai yang marah harus dibuang
Khabar Melayu seamat ramah Tindak-tanduk elak kan balah
Gurindam Pasal Kelima Jika mampir orang berdagang Titik perhati segala belang

Inilah akhir gurindam enam pasal yang dikarang oleh Otto Ali pada tahun 1263 Hijrah Nabi hingga dua puluh tiga hari bulan Sya'ban Kamis pukul 05.00 Negeri Hujung Manani."

Di dalam gurindam ini, saya mengungkapkan keseluruhan idea dan gagasan akal budi Melayu, dengan pesan besar bahawa terdapatnya musuh atau ancaman terhadap bangsa yang terdiri dalam bentuk pemerintah yang jahat, dan berpihak kepada yang korup; ulama yang tidak lagi menobatkan kebenaran dan keadilan; rakyat atau warga dilalaikan dengan candu dan madat; serta terakhir kumpulan saudagar kapitalis mementingkan haloba perut berbanding kesejahteraan umat.
Empat kelompok atau golongan yang menentukan arah baik dan buruknya negara ini bukanlah sesuatu yang boleh muncul secara tiba-tiba tentunya. Ia tiba dengan memori berjejak di dalam benak saya.
Enam pasal ingatan dalam gurindam ini dapat direnung dan dicermin kembali dalam pelbagai titah diraja oleh raja-raja Melayu.

Sebagai contoh tuntutan keadilan dan pesan agar raja sentiasa terpandu dinasihati, yang mana dalam konteks zaman moden kita di Malaysia adalah raja berpelembagaan sejajar dengan titah baginda Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir, Yang Dipertuan Besar Negeri Sembilan di Istiadat Pengurniaan Darjah Kebesaran, Bintang dan Pingat sempena Hari Keputeraan ke-78 baginda di Istana Besar Seri Menanti pada 14 Jan 2026.

"Rasuah merupakan musuh utama kepada keadilan, amanah dan masa depan negara. Beta amat terperanjat dan kecewa apabila masih wujud pihak yang terus memberikan sokongan kepada individu yang telah disabitkan bersalah atas tuduhan rasuah yang amat besar, seolah-olah perbuatan tersebut boleh diterima dan dimaafkan. Mereka yang masih menyokong penjenayah seperti ini agar segera bermuhasabah diri serta menilai semula pendirian dan kepercayaan masing-masing. Ini kerana sebarang bentuk toleransi atau kompromi terhadap rasuah adalah bertentangan dengan prinsip kebenaran, keadilan serta amanah dan sama sekali tidak boleh diterima dalam sebuah negara yang menjunjung kedaulatan undang-undang."

Tuanku Muhriz berasa khuatir sebarang toleransi dan kelonggaran kepada penjenayah dan jenayah rasuah boleh menjejaskan masa depan negara kita di mana keadilan dilihat tidak lagi dilaksanakan dengan setara, atau terdapat dwistandard antara kelas tertentu.

Baginda tidaklah bersendirian dalam menolak rasuah dan perasuah. Pada 22 Sept 2022 misalnya; Sultan Perak, Sultan Nazrin Muizzuddin Shah bertitah, ketika melancarkan buku tulisan M Kamal Hassan bertajuk 'Korupsi dan Kemunafikan Dalam Politik Melayu, Perlunya Disegerakan Transformasi Moral Etika', bahawa rasuah dikenal pasti sebagai salah satu sebab utama yang membantutkan pertumbuhan ekonomi, menghilangkan minat pelaburan asing, meningkatkan kos pentadbiran dan urus niaga, menidakkan rakyat daripada mendapat perkhidmatan, serta mendorong berlakunya ketidakstabilan politik.

Ingatan yang lebih jelas daripada Sultan Nazrin terpancar dalam titah baginda yang lebih mutakhir iaitu pada 2023, ketika Istiadat Menghadap Sembah Taat Setia dan Penganugerahan Darjah Kebesaran Negeri Perak Darul Ridzuan sempena sambutan Ulang Tahun Hari Keputeraan ke-66. Titah Sultan Nazrin lagi rakyat semakin lantang mendedahkan isu rasuah, gigih menolak pemimpin berimej rasuah dan menggunakan jawatan untuk kepentingan diri, atau pemimpin yang mengumpul kekayaan untuk ahli keluarga serta pemimpin yang menjadi instrumen kepada ahli perniagaan.

Saya mengimpikan Gurindam Enam akan menjadi sepertinya Gurindam Dua Belas, sebagai sebuah karya klasik yang bertahan zaman dan dihayati gagasan keseluruhannya seperti mana rakyat Hujung Manani lakukan di dalam novel Koro.

810cf766812e6045: “If that’s what the law says, then the law is an ass.”

These words are famously associated with Charles Dickens’ 1838 novel, Oliver Twist. However, the expression appeared in print much earlier, in the 1654 play Revenge of Honour: “The law is such an ass.”
It refers to the foolish or rigid application of the law when it defies common sense, humanity or reality.
This remains true today. Our legal ecosystem appears trapped in a time warp.
Consider a recent case in which the High Court rejected a man’s bid to secure Malaysian citizenship for his stateless son, despite DNA tests establishing their biological relationship.
The son has lived in Malaysia since he was three months old, has no birth certificate and has never held citizenship of any country.
Born in Thailand to a Malaysian father and Thai mother, he was ruled ineligible for citizenship by operation of law because his parents could not prove they were legally married when he was born.

The court held that Section 17 of Part III of the Second Schedule of the Federal Constitution applied, treating the child as born out of wedlock. Under that provision, references to the father of an illegitimate child are construed as references to the mother for citizenship purposes.
Unless the law changes, such inflexibility will remain. University students should examine such social issues, particularly cases involving children born out of wedlock.
Politics may prove even more confusing.

Many will recall a former federal minister convicted of murdering his political opponent in the 1980s. His death sentence was commuted to life imprisonment by the Pardons Board, and he was released about eight years later after receiving a royal pardon.

Does this mean society condones murder? Over the years, pardons have been granted to numerous convicted individuals on the merits of their cases, with few questions raised. Can it therefore be argued that society condones their crimes? Politicians and students alike should understand this distinction.

Fast-forward 30 years, and we are debating an unrelated corruption case in which the same discretionary powers of the Federal Territories Pardons Board (FTPB) have been exercised. Yet there are now claims that granting a pardon amounts to condoning corruption.

It is deeply saddening when such arguments come from senior political leaders, including the apparent political theatre surrounding a minister’s decision to step down on the day an individual moves into his home to serve the remainder of his sentence under house arrest.
The granting of pardons by the FTPB, chaired by the King, is part of the legal framework, following a process in which individuals are charged, convicted and sentenced after due process.
The law applies to everyone. Article 8 of the Federal Constitution guarantees equality before the law. Article 8(1) states that all persons are equal before the law and entitled to equal protection.
If the law applies when someone is convicted, it must also apply when a pardon is considered. Should a person be denied the opportunity to seek one because of his standing in society?

Why demand the minutes of an FTPB meeting or suggest something is amiss merely because of the individual involved? To do so without credible evidence implies that not everyone is equal before the law. Could the legal process itself also have been compromised because of the individual’s standing?

Questions have also been raised about the “donations” used to pay the fine, with aspersions cast over their source. These were funds belonging to a political party. Why should anyone dictate how another party uses its funds if they are not members?
We appear blinded by political opportunism, bordering on vengeance. What matters is the spirit of the law.

The recent actions of the Attorney-General’s Chambers (AGC) in Najib Razak’s case have left a bitter aftertaste, regardless of the legal questions surrounding errors in court documents, apparently caused by a lack of scrutiny.
This begs the question: who is the ass here – the law, the drafters, those responsible for scrutinising the documents or those interpreting the discharge order?
Why was the issue raised at the last minute, despite the legal arguments over the wording of the discharge order? Many are now up in arms over the AGC’s position.

This has fuelled interpretations of the motives behind the move. When one institution has two functions – advising the government and acting as public prosecutor – perceptions can easily become tainted.
As a nation, we remain trapped in a political time warp of unholy alliances, racial and religious slurs, and relentless backstabbing, at the expense of more pressing issues.
All parties must stop linking the royal pardon and house-arrest arrangement to condoning corruption. It is demeaning.
A royal decree is a royal decree. We must live with it, while one particular individual gets on with finding another day job.
